about: Dated finds of Homo sapiens and its relatives, each as its source reports it, hand-curated for histeclipse. Dates are thousands of years ago; places are rounded to 0.1°. Where finds are argued over, competing claims share a question.

claims.claim: LD 350-1, a jaw that is the oldest known fossil of our genus, 2.75 to 2.80 million years old.
claims.found: The left half of a lower jaw with five teeth, mixing traits of Australopithecus and later Homo.
claims.dating: Argon–argon dating of volcanic ash layers above and below the fossil.
claims.discovered: Found in 2013 by Chalachew Seyoum, a student on the Ledi-Geraru project.
claims.matters: It pushes the fossil record of Homo back by about 400,000 years, to soon after the last Lucy-like australopiths in the same region.

evidence.text: DiMaggio et al. studied the sediments and ash layers of Ledi-Geraru, confirmed the ancient date of the site, and found the setting more open and arid than once thought.
Hawks et al. argued that some Australopithecus sediba data used in the study were wrong and that, with correct data, LD 350-1 cannot be assigned to Homo with certainty.

claims.question: homo-out-of-africa
claims.claim: Stone tools on the Chinese Loess Plateau from about 2.1 million years ago, the oldest sign of humans outside Africa if the dating holds.
claims.found: Stone tools in 17 layers of wind-blown loess and ancient soils; no human bones.
claims.dating: Palaeomagnetism and the loess–soil sequence, from loess L28 (about 2.12 million years) to soil S15 (about 1.26 million).
claims.discovered: Reported in 2018 by a team led by Zhu Zhaoyu.
claims.matters: If right, humans left Africa before Dmanisi’s people; with no bones, which species made the tools is unknown.

claims.claim: KNM-ER 1470, the skull that defines Homo rudolfensis, between 1.95 and 2.06 million years old.

source.citation: Joordens et al. 2013, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: A larger-brained skull with a long, flat face, pieced together from many fragments.
claims.dating: Palaeomagnetism and strontium isotope stratigraphy of the upper Burgi Member, Koobi Fora.
claims.discovered: Found in 1972 by Bernard Ngeneo, of Richard Leakey’s team.
claims.matters: It suggests two or more kinds of early Homo lived side by side near 2 million years ago; some still place it in Homo habilis.

evidence.text: Leakey et al. described three new fossils, 1.78 to 1.95 million years old, that match the face and jaw of KNM-ER 1470, and took them to confirm two species of early Homo.
Spoor et al. reconstructed the OH 7 jaw and found it incompatible with fossils assigned to Homo rudolfensis, supporting more than one species of early Homo.
Wood and Collard reviewed the criteria for the genus Homo and concluded that Homo rudolfensis, like Homo habilis, does not belong in Homo.

claims.claim: DNH 134, a child’s skull read as the oldest Homo erectus, 1.95 to 2.04 million years old.
claims.found: The back of a young child’s skull with affinities to Homo erectus, from the same cave as a Paranthropus skull.
claims.dating: Uranium–lead dating of flowstone, palaeomagnetism and ESR on teeth.
claims.discovered: Found in 2015; reported in 2020 by Andy Herries and colleagues.
claims.matters: Homo erectus, Paranthropus and Australopithecus lived together here about 2 million years ago; some doubt a skull this young can be assigned with confidence.

evidence.text: Martin et al. described 18 more skull and jaw fossils from Drimolen and assigned one, DNH 127, to Homo erectus, adding evidence for the species there about 1.95 to 2.04 million years ago.

source.citation: Martin et al. 2026, Annals of Human Biology

evidence.text: Zanolli et al. studied the inner structure of teeth assigned to early Homo at Drimolen and nearby sites; only 4 of 23 were clearly Homo, none from Drimolen.

claims.claim: OH 7, the type fossil of Homo habilis, from Bed I at Olduvai, about 1.8 million years old.
claims.found: A juvenile’s lower jaw with 13 teeth, parts of the skull and 21 hand and wrist bones.
claims.dating: Argon–argon dates for the Bed I tuffs: Tuff IB at 1.848 and Tuff IF at 1.803 million years.
claims.discovered: Found in November 1960 by Jonathan Leakey; named Homo habilis by Louis Leakey, Phillip Tobias and John Napier in 1964.
claims.matters: It defined Homo habilis, ‘handy man’, the first species placed in Homo on a small brain; whether habilis belongs in Homo is still argued.

evidence.text: Spoor et al. rebuilt the distorted OH 7 jaw virtually and found it primitive and distinct from Homo rudolfensis, suggesting the habilis lineage began before 2.3 million years ago.
Wood and Collard reviewed the criteria for the genus Homo and concluded that Homo habilis, named from OH 7, should not be placed in Homo.

claims.question: homo-out-of-africa
claims.claim: The oldest human fossils outside Africa: people at Dmanisi from soon after 1.85 million years ago, the skulls about 1.77 million.
claims.found: Five skulls, jaws and skeletal remains of small-brained early humans, with stone tools.
claims.dating: Argon–argon dating of volcanic rocks and palaeomagnetism of the layers.
claims.discovered: The first jaw was found in 1991; Skull 5 was published in 2013 by David Lordkipanidze and colleagues.
claims.matters: The skulls vary so much that some read them, and early Homo generally, as one variable species; others name them Homo georgicus.

evidence.text: Gabunia et al. described two skulls like early African Homo erectus and found that fossils, geochronology and palaeomagnetism all pointed to about 1.7 million years.
Lordkipanidze et al. described Skull 5, the first complete skull from this period, and read the five Dmanisi skulls as one regional variant of Homo erectus.
Schwartz et al. replied that the teeth, jaws and skulls suggest more than one kind of hominin at Dmanisi, and that the name Homo georgicus is valid.

claims.claim: Turkana Boy, the most complete early human skeleton, about 1.6 million years old.
claims.found: KNM-WT 15000, a nearly complete skeleton of a youth, already about 1.6 m tall.
claims.dating: From the dated layers of the Nachukui Formation at Nariokotome III.
claims.discovered: Found in 1984 by Kamoya Kimeu, of Richard Leakey and Alan Walker’s team.
claims.matters: It showed a body built like ours for walking and heat; some name the African form Homo ergaster.

evidence.text: Graves et al. modelled other growth patterns for KNM-WT 15000 and estimated he would have reached about 163 cm as an adult, not 185 cm as previously reported.

source.citation: Graves et al. 2010, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: Homo erectus first appears at Sangiran about 1.3 million years ago, later than once thought.
claims.found: More than 100 Homo erectus fossils, about half of all those known.
claims.dating: Fission-track and uranium–lead dating of zircons in the volcanic layers below the oldest fossils.
claims.discovered: From 1936, by Ralph von Koenigswald and later by Indonesian teams.
claims.matters: It moves the first people on Java to about 1.3 million years ago and less than 1.5 million, against the 1.5–1.6 million long accepted.

evidence.text: Swisher et al. argon-dated pumice from two Sangiran hominin sites to 1.81 and 1.66 million years, much older than the 1.3 million years in this claim.
Larick et al. doubted where those samples came from and dated pumice with fossils in southeast Sangiran to 1.51–1.02 million years, with four skulls at about 1.25 million.

claims.claim: A jaw from Sima del Elefante, about 1.1 to 1.2 million years old, then the oldest human in western Europe.
claims.found: Part of a lower jaw (ATE9-1) with simple stone tools and cut-marked animal bones.
claims.dating: Palaeomagnetism, cosmogenic nuclides and the fauna of level TE9.
claims.discovered: The jaw was found in 2007; a partial face, ATE7-1, in 2022.
claims.matters: Carbonell et al. linked it to the Gran Dolina lineage; Huguet et al. (2025) read the older face from level TE7 as Homo aff. erectus, not antecessor.

evidence.text: Huguet et al. described most of a face, ATE7-1, from the lower level TE7 of the same site, 1.1 to 1.4 million years old, and assigned it to Homo aff. erectus.

claims.claim: Footprints of a small group on a river estuary, between 780,000 and 1 million years old; the oldest outside Africa.
claims.found: About 50 footprints of adults and children in laminated silts, with flint tools nearby.
claims.dating: Palaeomagnetism and the fauna and flora of the Early Pleistocene deposits.
claims.discovered: Exposed by the sea in May 2013 and recorded by a team led by Nick Ashton before they eroded away.
claims.matters: No bones were found; the authors suggest Homo antecessor, the only human of similar age known in western Europe.

evidence.text: Parfitt et al. found stone tools at Happisburgh showing hominins in northern Europe more than 780,000 years ago, at the southern edge of the boreal zone.
Wiseman et al. compared the shapes of the prints with other hominin tracks and found them closest to presumed Homo erectus prints from Ileret, Kenya.

source.citation: Wiseman et al. 2020, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: Homo antecessor at Gran Dolina, between 772,000 and 949,000 years ago.
claims.found: Over 170 bones and teeth from at least eight people, many with cut marks; a child’s face looks strikingly modern.
claims.dating: ESR and uranium-series on a human tooth, with palaeomagnetism of layer TD6.
claims.discovered: Found from 1994 by the Atapuerca team; named in 1997 by José María Bermúdez de Castro and colleagues.
claims.matters: Among the oldest humans in western Europe; the cut marks are read as the earliest evidence of cannibalism.

evidence.text: Parés and Pérez-González measured the magnetism of the Gran Dolina sediments and found the human layer TD6 was laid down more than 780,000 years ago.
Falguères et al. dated teeth by ESR and uranium-series and confirmed that TD6 belongs to the end of the Early Pleistocene, as the palaeomagnetism suggested.

source.citation: Falguères et al. 1999, Journal of Human Evolution

evidence.text: Welker et al. read ancient proteins from a Homo antecessor tooth and found it a close sister lineage to later humans, including Neanderthals, Denisovans and us.
Bermúdez de Castro et al. described the TD6 fossils and named them a new species, Homo antecessor, with a mid-face like that of modern humans.

source.citation: Bermúdez de Castro et al. 1997, Science

claims.claim: Peking Man’s lower layers, about 770,000 years old.
claims.found: Skulls, teeth and bones of some 40 Homo erectus individuals, with stone tools; the originals were lost in 1941.
claims.dating: Aluminium-26 and beryllium-10 burial dating of quartz in layers 7–10: 0.77 ± 0.08 million years.
claims.discovered: First teeth from 1921; the first skull found in 1929 by Pei Wenzhong.
claims.matters: Older than long assumed, it puts Homo erectus in northern China through a mild glacial period.

evidence.text: Grün et al. ESR-dated teeth from layers 3, 6/7 and 10 and found 300,000 to 550,000 years for the Homo erectus remains, younger than this claim.

source.citation: Grün et al. 1997, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: Jaw and teeth like Homo floresiensis but about 700,000 years old.
claims.found: A jaw fragment and six teeth from at least three small individuals, with stone tools.
claims.dating: Argon–argon and fission-track dates on volcanic layers above and below, with US-ESR on teeth.
claims.discovered: Found in 2014 by an Indonesian–Australian team led by Gerrit van den Bergh.
claims.matters: Van den Bergh et al. read them as dwarfed descendants of Homo erectus; Argue et al. (2017) argue for an older lineage nearer Homo habilis.

evidence.text: van den Bergh et al. described the Mata Menge jaw and six teeth, about 700,000 years old, and found them like those of Homo floresiensis, but even smaller.

source.citation: van den Bergh et al. 2016, Nature

evidence.text: Kaifu et al. reported an adult arm bone from the same deposits, smaller than that of Homo floresiensis, and concluded the lineage was tiny by about 700,000 years ago.
Brumm et al. described 507 stone tools from Mata Menge, dated to 840,000–700,000 years ago, and noted continuity with tools of Homo floresiensis at Liang Bua.

claims.claim: The Mauer jaw, type fossil of Homo heidelbergensis, about 609,000 years old.
claims.found: A robust lower jaw with all its teeth, from river sands of the Neckar.
claims.dating: ESR/uranium-series on mammal teeth and infrared radiofluorescence on sand grains: 609 ± 40 thousand years.
claims.discovered: Found in 1907 by the sand-pit worker Daniel Hartmann; named by Otto Schoetensack in 1908.
claims.matters: The oldest human fossil from central and northern Europe; which later fossils belong with it is still argued.

evidence.text: Mounier et al. compared the Mauer jaw with 36 Pleistocene fossils and found Homo heidelbergensis a valid species, most likely the last common ancestor of Neanderthals and us.

source.citation: Mounier et al. 2009, Journal of Human Evolution

evidence.text: Roksandic et al. argued that the name Homo heidelbergensis is poorly defined and should be dropped, with many western European fossils moved to the Neanderthals.

claims.claim: The Bodo skull from the Middle Awash, about 600,000 years old.
claims.found: A large face and braincase with cut marks, perhaps from defleshing.
claims.dating: Argon–argon dating, tephra correlation and the fauna of the layers.
claims.discovered: Found in 1976 by a team of the Rift Valley Research Mission in Ethiopia.
claims.matters: A large-brained African human of the Middle Pleistocene; some place it in Homo heidelbergensis, others in Homo rhodesiensis.

evidence.text: Roksandic et al. proposed a new species, Homo bodoensis, named after Bodo, as an early Middle Pleistocene African ancestor of Homo sapiens.
Delson and Stringer rejected Homo bodoensis, arguing that the renaming breaks the rules of zoological nomenclature and does not resolve the wider debate.

claims.claim: Java Man’s layer at Trinil, 430,000 to 540,000 years old, with a shell engraved by Homo erectus.
claims.found: The skullcap and thigh bone of Java Man; in the same layer, freshwater shells, one used as a tool, one engraved with a zigzag.
claims.dating: Argon–argon and luminescence dating of sediment inside the shells.
claims.discovered: Found in 1891–1892 by Eugène Dubois; the engraving was noticed in his collection in 2007.
claims.matters: Java Man was the first Homo erectus found; the engraving, if made by erectus, is the oldest known.

evidence.text: Hilgen et al. found two fossil-rich channels at Trinil, one 830,000–773,000 years old and one about 450,000–430,000, and suggested Dubois dug fossils from layers of different ages.

source.citation: Hilgen et al. 2023, Quaternary Science Reviews

claims.claim: At least 28 people at the bottom of a cave shaft, at least about 430,000 years old.

source.citation: Arnold et al. 2014, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: About 7,000 bones from at least 28 individuals, with a single hand axe.
claims.dating: Luminescence dating of overlying sediments (minimum 427 ± 12 thousand years) and palaeomagnetism.
claims.discovered: First human remains found in 1976; dug systematically since 1984 by Juan Luis Arsuaga’s team.
claims.matters: Long called heidelbergensis; Arsuaga et al. (2014) find early Neanderthal traits, and their nuclear DNA (Meyer et al. 2016) is closer to Neanderthals.

evidence.text: Bischoff et al. reported high-resolution uranium-series dates giving the hominins an age of about 600,000 years (minus 66,000, no upper limit), older than this claim.

source.citation: Bischoff et al. 2007, Journal of Archaeological Science

evidence.text: Meyer et al. recovered nuclear DNA from two individuals and found them related to Neanderthals rather than Denisovans, so the two groups split before 430,000 years ago.
Arsuaga et al. studied 17 skulls from the site and found Neanderthal-like features, placing these people on the Neanderthal line nearly half a million years ago.

claims.claim: The oldest known fossils of our species, about 315,000 years old.
claims.found: Skull, face, jaws, teeth and some limb bones of at least five people, with Middle Stone Age stone tools
claims.dating: Thermoluminescence of heated flints (about 315,000 years), and uranium-series and electron spin resonance dating of a tooth
claims.discovered: Found by barite miners in 1961; re-excavated from 2004 by a team led by Jean-Jacques Hublin and Abdelouahed Ben-Ncer
claims.matters: The oldest fossils assigned to Homo sapiens. Faces and teeth are like ours, but braincases are long and low, so Hublin et al. read our species as older, and its origin as spread across Africa.

evidence.text: Richter et al. dated heated flints by thermoluminescence to 315,000 ± 34,000 years, and recalculated a tooth date to 286,000 ± 32,000, almost double earlier estimates.
Smith et al. scanned the teeth of a juvenile from Jebel Irhoud, then dated to 160,000 years, and found a modern human pace of dental development.

claims.claim: Homo naledi in the Dinaledi Chamber, between 236,000 and 335,000 years ago.
claims.found: Over 1,500 bones of at least 15 small-brained individuals, deep in a cave reached only by narrow passages.
claims.dating: Uranium–thorium on flowstones, luminescence on sediments and US-ESR on three teeth.
claims.discovered: Found in 2013 by the cavers Steven Tucker and Rick Hunter; recovered by Lee Berger’s team.
claims.matters: A small-brained species alive when our own was emerging; Berger’s team say it buried its dead, which other researchers dispute.

evidence.text: Berger et al. described at least 15 individuals from the Dinaledi Chamber and named Homo naledi, with a small brain but humanlike hands and feet.
Hawks et al. reported 131 more Homo naledi specimens from a second chamber, Lesedi, including a near-complete skull of about 610 ml.

claims.claim: The Kabwe skull, about 299,000 years old, much younger than long thought.
claims.found: One of the best preserved fossil skulls, with a heavy brow and many tooth cavities.
claims.dating: Uranium-series and ESR dating directly on the skull and associated bones: 299 ± 25 thousand years.
claims.discovered: Found in 1921 by the miner Tom Zwiglaar in the Broken Hill lead and zinc mine.
claims.matters: Type fossil of Homo rhodesiensis, often placed in heidelbergensis; it lived at the same time as early Homo sapiens and Homo naledi.

evidence.text: Roksandic et al. argued that Homo rhodesiensis, the name based on this skull, is poorly defined and should be abandoned in favour of a new species, Homo bodoensis.
Delson and Stringer defended Homo rhodesiensis, named by Woodward in 1921, and rejected Homo bodoensis as a junior synonym.

claims.claim: Early Neanderthal teeth about 300,000 years old, the earliest Neanderthal evidence in the region according to Radović et al.

source.citation: Radović et al. 2025, American Journal of Biological Anthropology

claims.found: Teeth from layers 3a and 3b; a third molar, BH-15, has a mid-trigonid crest, a trait seen as diagnostic of the Neanderthal lineage.
claims.dating: Layer 3a dated by thermoluminescence to 285,000 ± 34,000 and 295,000 ± 74,000 years.
claims.matters: Radović et al. say the finds reinforce early Neanderthal presence here around 300,000 years ago, while the nearby Mala Balanica jaw lacks Neanderthal traits.

evidence.text: Mihailović et al. dated layer 3 at Velika Balanica to MIS 9–7 with TL and ESR, and found tools resembling the Yabrudian of the Levant.

source.citation: Mihailović et al. 2022, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: The Harbin skull, at least 146,000 years old, named Homo longi in 2021.
claims.found: A nearly complete, very large skull with a big brain and heavy brow.
claims.dating: Uranium-series on the skull (over 146,000 years) and geochemical matching to a layer dated 138,000–309,000 by OSL.
claims.discovered: Found in 1933 by a labourer building a bridge in Harbin; hidden in a well and handed over in 2018.
claims.matters: Ji et al. (2021) named it Homo longi; ancient proteins and mitochondrial DNA (Fu et al. 2025) place it among the Denisovans.

evidence.text: Ni et al. ran phylogenetic analyses and found that the Harbin skull, with fossils such as Dali and Xiahe, forms a third human lineage in East Asia.
Fu et al. recovered 95 proteins from the skull; three Denisovan-derived variants placed the Harbin individual in a Denisovan population.
Fu et al. retrieved mitochondrial DNA from dental calculus on the skull; it falls within Denisovan variation, close to early Denisovans from Denisova Cave.

claims.claim: The Florisbad skull, about 259,000 years old.
claims.found: Part of a skull with much of the face, from a spring mound.
claims.dating: ESR dating directly on a tooth from the skull: 259 ± 35 thousand years.
claims.discovered: Found in 1932 by T. F. Dreyer, who named it Homo helmei.
claims.matters: Its place is argued: an early Homo sapiens to some, a late Homo heidelbergensis or helmei to others.

evidence.text: Berger and Hawks reviewed the excavation records, doubted that the dated tooth and the skull belong together, and concluded the data do not show Homo sapiens there at about 260,000 years.

claims.claim: Neanderthal remains, many from children, in layers dated to 273,000–146,000 years ago, among the earliest Neanderthals in Iberia.
claims.found: Cranial and skeletal remains of at least seven individuals, four of them children under ten, with Mousterian tools.
claims.dating: ESR/U-series on herbivore teeth from four layers: occupation in MIS 8 to 6, between 273 ± 26 ka and 146 ± 34 ka.
claims.matters: Richard et al. say the site is about 100,000 years older than earlier sediment TL dates suggested, which would make it one of the first Neanderthal sites in Iberia.

evidence.text: Arsuaga et al. described new remains and found diagnostic Neanderthal features, concluding all the Cova Negra humans are Neanderthals.

source.citation: Arsuaga et al. 2007, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: Omo I, the oldest Homo sapiens known from eastern Africa: at least 233,000 years old.
claims.found: Omo I: parts of a skull, jaw and skeleton of one person, from the Kibish Formation by the Omo River
claims.dating: Chemical match of a volcanic ash above the fossil to an eruption of Shala volcano, dated by argon-argon to about 233,000 years
claims.discovered: Found in 1967 by a team led by Richard Leakey; the site was re-studied by Céline Vidal and colleagues
claims.matters: Gives a minimum age, older than the earlier estimate of about 195,000 years, for one of the first fossils with a fully modern skull shape.

evidence.text: McDougall et al. argon-dated a tuff they placed below Omo I and II and preferred an age of 195,000 ± 5,000 years: an earlier, younger estimate than this claim.
Brown et al. matched the KHS Tuff of the Kibish Formation with ash layers elsewhere in Ethiopia and found support for an age near 196,000 years for Omo I and II.

source.citation: Brown et al. 2012, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: Early Neanderthal remains from the lower travertine at Ehringsdorf, which U-series dating puts at about 230,000 years old.
claims.found: Hominin remains in the lower travertine, a limestone laid down in an interglacial.
claims.dating: U-series on travertine: apparent ages from over 350,000 to 200,000 years; the best estimate is about 230,000 years (MIS 7).
claims.matters: Blackwell & Schwarcz’s dates moved the lower travertine from the last interglacial to MIS 7. Urciuoli et al. call Ehringsdorf one of the earliest Neanderthals, whose affinities are still argued.

evidence.text: Urciuoli et al. found that the Ehringsdorf and Reilingen inner ears are almost fully like late Neanderthals, though both fossils’ affinities have been contentious.

source.citation: Urciuoli et al. 2025, The Anatomical Record

claims.claim: Seventeen hominin teeth about 225,000 years old, closest to Sima de los Huesos and placed in an early stage of Neanderthal evolution.

source.citation: Compton & Stringer 2015, Journal of Quaternary Science

claims.found: 17 hominin teeth with handaxe and Levallois tools.
claims.dating: Probable age of about 225,000 years, as given by Compton & Stringer.
claims.discovered: Excavated between 1980 and 1995.
claims.matters: Compton & Stringer place the teeth in the pre-Neanderthal stage and reject assigning them to Homo heidelbergensis, a view others have held.

claims.question: first-out-of-africa
claims.claim: A skull fragment read as Homo sapiens, over 210,000 years old; the reading is disputed.
claims.found: Apidima 1, the back of a skull, found in one block of breccia with Apidima 2, a more complete skull with a face
claims.dating: Uranium-series dating of the skull bone itself: Apidima 1 over 210,000 years, Apidima 2 over 170,000 years
claims.discovered: Found in 1978 by a University of Athens team led by Theodoros Pitsios; studied by Katerina Harvati’s team with CT scans
claims.matters: Harvati et al. read Apidima 1 as Homo sapiens, the oldest outside Africa. Others, e.g. de Lumley et al. 2020, read both skulls as pre-Neanderthal and question the dating.

evidence.text: de Lumley et al. dated both skulls by uranium–thorium to 220,000–130,000 years and read both as evolved European Homo erectus with early Neanderthal traits, not Homo sapiens.
Bartsiokas et al. dated a fragment of Apidima 2 by U-series to at least 160,000 years and judged its face to belong to the Neanderthal clade.

source.citation: Bartsiokas et al. 2017, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: Denisovans at the cave by about 200,000 years ago; the group is known mainly from its genome.
claims.found: Bone fragments and teeth of Denisovans and Neanderthals, and a child of both, with stone tools, and ancient DNA in the sediment
claims.dating: Radiocarbon, optical dating of sediments and genetic ages, combined in a statistical model
claims.discovered: Dug since the late 1970s by Novosibirsk teams led by Anatoly Derevianko and Michael Shunkov; the Denisovan finger bone was found in 2008
claims.matters: Denisovans were named from the DNA of a finger bone here in 2010. Douka et al. and Jacobs et al. 2019 date them at the cave from about 200,000 to about 50,000 years ago.

evidence.text: Jacobs et al. built an optical dating chronology for the cave sediments and traced hominin occupation from about 300,000 to 20,000 years ago.
Zavala et al. found Denisovan mitochondrial DNA in sediments with early Middle Palaeolithic tools about 250,000–170,000 years old, before any Neanderthal DNA.
Reich et al. sequenced the genome of a finger bone from the cave, named the group Denisovans, and found they gave 4–6% of the DNA of present-day Melanesians.
Prüfer et al. sequenced a high-quality genome of a Neanderthal woman from the Altai, whose parents were related at about the level of half-siblings.
Mafessoni et al. found the Chagyrskaya Neanderthal closer to western Neanderthals than to the earlier Neanderthals of Denisova Cave, about 100 km away.
Kolobova et al. note earlier Neanderthals at other Altai sites without Micoquian-like tools, implying two or more Neanderthal arrivals in the region.

claims.claim: The most complete Palaeolithic wooden spears, which Hutson et al. redate to about 200,000 years and link to Neanderthals; earlier estimates were 400,000 and 300,000 years.
claims.found: Wooden throwing spears and double-pointed sticks, with stone tools and butchered horses, by an ancient lakeshore.
claims.dating: Amino acid dating of fossils from the Spear Horizon and a regional reassessment give about 200,000 years (Hutson et al.).
claims.discovered: The spears were found in 1995, as reported by Thieme 1997.
claims.matters: The age decides who made the spears. Thieme proposed about 400,000 years and Richter & Krbetschek 337,000–300,000; Hutson et al.’s 200,000 years places them among Middle Palaeolithic Neanderthals.

evidence.text: Thieme described the spears as about 400,000 years old and the oldest complete hunting weapons then known.
Richter & Krbetschek dated heated flint from a nearby Schöningen site to 321,000 ± 16,000 years and inferred 337,000–300,000 years for the spears.

source.citation: Richter & Krbetschek 2015, Journal of Human Evolution

evidence.text: Milks et al. analysed a double-pointed stick from the site, then dated to about 300,000 years, and found skilled woodworking for a hunting throwing stick.

claims.question: first-out-of-africa
claims.claim: A modern human jaw, 177,000 to 194,000 years old.
claims.found: Misliya-1, an adult’s left upper jaw with most of its teeth, with Levallois stone tools
claims.dating: Uranium-series and electron spin resonance of the teeth, uranium-series of crusts on the jaw, and thermoluminescence of burnt flints
claims.discovered: Found in 2002 during excavations led by Mina Weinstein-Evron (University of Haifa); described by Israel Hershkovitz and colleagues
claims.matters: Hershkovitz et al. read it as the oldest modern human fossil outside Africa, putting our species in the Levant 50,000 years earlier than thought. Its age is older than Qafzeh; the Apidima claim is older still.

evidence.text: Valladas et al. dated 32 burnt flints by thermoluminescence and placed Misliya’s Early Middle Palaeolithic layers at about 250,000 to 160,000 years ago.

source.citation: Valladas et al. 2013, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: Penghu 1, a jaw dredged from the sea floor off Taiwan, identified as a Denisovan man; 10,000–70,000 or 130,000–190,000 years old.
claims.found: A robust lower jaw with teeth; ancient proteins identify it as male and Denisovan.
claims.dating: Not dated directly; the ages come from the fauna dredged with it and from times of low sea level.
claims.discovered: Recovered by fishermen in the Penghu Channel; bought by Kun-Yu Tsai in an antique shop and first described in 2015.
claims.matters: It puts Denisovans in warm, humid lowlands far from Siberia and Tibet, and shows their robust jaws and large teeth.

evidence.text: Chang et al. first described the jaw as archaic Homo with robust, primitive features, younger than 450,000 and most likely 190,000–10,000 years old.

claims.claim: Rings of broken stalagmites built 336 m inside Bruniquel Cave about 176,500 years ago, with traces of fire.
claims.found: Ring-shaped structures of broken stalagmites, with traces of fire and burnt bone, deep in the cave.
claims.dating: U-series dates on stalagmite regrowths and burnt bone, with the tips of the broken stalagmites: 176.5 ± 2.1 ka.
claims.matters: Jaubert et al. call these among the oldest well-dated human constructions and say their builders had mastered the underground world. Their purpose is unknown.

evidence.text: Aubert et al. list the Bruniquel structures among Neanderthal behaviours whose meaning divides scientific opinion.

source.citation: Aubert et al. 2018, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: A nearly complete Neanderthal skeleton encased in calcite, dated to between 172,000 and 130,000 years ago.

source.citation: Lari et al. 2015, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: A whole skeleton stuck in calcite concretions; a shoulder blade fragment was removed for study.
claims.dating: First dating of the skeleton, from a retrieved bone fragment and its setting: 172 ± 15 ka to 130.1 ± 1.9 ka.
claims.discovered: Found in 1993 during a caving survey.
claims.matters: Lari et al. call it the oldest Neanderthal with endogenous DNA. Buzi et al. (2025) describe its nose, the first complete inner nasal cavity in the fossil record.

evidence.text: Buzi et al. describe the complete inner nasal structures of this early Neanderthal, testing traits once proposed as cold adaptations.
Riga et al. used a videoscope to describe the nearly complete teeth, with a retromolar space and other features consistent with Neanderthals.

claims.claim: A Neanderthal from Scladina, about 120,000 years old, gave mtDNA and some nuclear DNA.
claims.found: Scladina I-4A, a Neanderthal.
claims.dating: About 120,000 years from mtDNA branch length (95% range 76,000–168,000).
claims.matters: With HST, it suggests later Neanderthals descend at least partly from these early Europeans (Peyrégne et al.).

evidence.text: Bokelmann et al. found the Forbes’ Quarry Neanderthal genetically closest to Scladina, HST and Mezmaiskaya 1.

claims.claim: A molar most likely Denisovan, 131,000 to 164,000 years old.
claims.found: One lower molar of a child, likely a girl, in cave breccia with animal teeth
claims.dating: Luminescence of the sediment, uranium-series of an overlying flowstone, and uranium-series–ESR of animal teeth
claims.discovered: Found in 2018 in Cobra Cave by a Lao–French–international team incl. Fabrice Demeter and Laura Shackelford
claims.matters: Demeter et al. read it as most likely Denisovan from its likeness to the Xiahe jaw; enamel proteins confirm only the genus Homo. If so, Denisovans lived in tropical Southeast Asia.

claims.claim: A Denisovan jaw at 3,280 m, at least 160,000 years old.
claims.found: The right half of a lower jaw with two molars (the Xiahe mandible)
claims.dating: Uranium-series dating of a carbonate crust on the jaw, at least 160,000 years; identified as Denisovan from ancient proteins in a molar
claims.discovered: Found in 1980 by a Buddhist monk in the cave; studied by Fahu Chen, Frido Welker, Jean-Jacques Hublin and colleagues
claims.matters: The first Denisovan fossil found outside Denisova Cave. It shows they lived at high altitude long before modern humans, which may explain a high-altitude gene Tibetans inherited from them.

evidence.text: Zhang et al. found Denisovan mitochondrial DNA in the cave sediments from about 100,000 and 60,000 years ago, and possibly 45,000.
Xia et al. identified a rib from the cave as Denisovan from its proteins, about 48,000–32,000 years old, and found Denisovans butchered wild sheep, goats and other animals.

claims.claim: Herto Man, early Homo sapiens skulls 154,000 to 160,000 years old.
claims.found: Crania of two adults and a child, with cut marks suggesting mortuary practice, and butchered hippo bones.
claims.dating: Argon–argon dating of the volcanic layers of the Upper Herto Member.
claims.discovered: Found in 1997 by the Middle Awash project team; described in 2003 by Tim White and colleagues.
claims.matters: Among the oldest well-dated fossils of our species; White et al. named them a subspecies, Homo sapiens idaltu.

evidence.text: White et al. described the Herto skulls, dated to 160,000–154,000 years, as between archaic Africans and later modern humans, and the likely ancestors of modern humans.

claims.claim: Shellfish, mainly mussels, collected through the Middle Palaeolithic levels of a sequence spanning about 160,000 to 35,000 years ago.

source.citation: Cortés-Sánchez et al. 2019, Quaternary Science Reviews

claims.found: Shellfish remains, mainly Mediterranean mussel, in Middle and early Upper Palaeolithic levels.
claims.dating: The sequence spans about 160–35 kyr cal BP, as given by Cortés-Sánchez et al.
claims.matters: Cortés-Sánchez et al. show shellfish collecting through MIS 4, a poorly known stage, and a long stable focus on mussels.

evidence.text: Zilhão et al. report large shell middens left by Last Interglacial Neanderthals at Figueira Brava, Portugal.

claims.claim: The largest Neanderthal assemblage from one site, about 130,000 years old.
claims.found: Some 900 bones and teeth from dozens of individuals, many broken and cut-marked; also eagle talons perhaps worn as jewellery.
claims.dating: ESR dating of animal tooth enamel: about 130 ± 10 thousand years.
claims.discovered: Excavated in 1899–1905 by Dragutin Gorjanović-Kramberger.
claims.matters: A rare look at a whole Neanderthal population; the cut marks are read as cannibalism or as mortuary treatment.

evidence.text: Radovčić et al. described eight cut-marked white-tailed eagle talons from one Krapina level, about 130,000 years old, and read them as Neanderthal jewellery.

claims.claim: Denisova 11, ‘Denny’, the daughter of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father, 80,000 to 140,000 years old.
claims.found: A bone fragment from a girl at least 13 years old, picked out among animal bones by its collagen.
claims.dating: Bayesian age model combining radiocarbon, uranium-series, optical and genetic data.
claims.discovered: Excavated in 2012 by Russian archaeologists; identified as human in 2016 by Samantha Brown.
claims.matters: Her genome (Slon et al. 2018) is the first of a first-generation cross between two human groups, so mixing was likely common when they met.

evidence.text: Slon et al. sequenced the genome of Denisova 11 and found she had a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father.
Brown et al. found the bone among more than 2,000 fragments by collagen fingerprinting; it carried Neanderthal-type mitochondrial DNA and was over 50,000 radiocarbon years old.

claims.question: nesher-ramla-homo
claims.claim: Nesher Ramla Homo: a skull fragment and jaw 120,000–140,000 years old that Hershkovitz et al. read as a late Middle Pleistocene Homo group.
claims.found: Part of a skull and a lower jaw, with stone tools and the bones of hunted animals.
claims.dating: Radiometric ages for the layers of 140,000 to 120,000 years, presented in the companion paper by Zaidner et al.
claims.discovered: Excavated in a quarry near Ramla by a team led by Yossi Zaidner; described in 2021.
claims.matters: The authors name no species; the site shows it under heidelbergensis as the nearest group. They see it as a source population for Neanderthals; Marom & Rak 2021 say it is simply a Neanderthal.

evidence.text: Zaidner et al. report that these people hunted large and small game, kept fires, cooked meat and used tools once linked only to Homo sapiens or Neanderthals.
Marom and Rak argue the jaw clearly shows the diagnostic features of a Neanderthal mandible, and that the fossils represent simply a Neanderthal.
May et al. replied that Marom and Rak used only a few jaw features and could not get beyond a choice between Neanderthal and modern human.

claims.question: nesher-ramla-homo
claims.claim: The Nesher Ramla fossils read as a Neanderthal, 120,000–140,000 years old, by Marom and Rak.
claims.found: The same jaw and skull fragment, which Marom and Rak say show the key features of a Neanderthal lower jaw.
claims.dating: The same layers, dated to 140,000–120,000 years ago by Zaidner et al. 2021.
claims.discovered: Excavated in a quarry near Ramla; the original description is Hershkovitz et al. 2021.
claims.matters: If Neanderthal, the find places Neanderthals in the southern Levant by about 130,000 years ago. Hershkovitz’s team (May et al. 2021) rejects this reading.

evidence.text: Hershkovitz et al. describe the fossils as a previously unknown archaic Homo group, among the last of Middle Pleistocene Homo.
May et al. say the comment lacks substance and was limited to a choice between Neanderthal and modern human.

claims.question: tabun-age
claims.claim: Tabun C1, a Neanderthal woman, about 122,000 years old if she belongs to layer C, as Grün and Stringer argue.

source.citation: Grün & Stringer 2000, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: A near-complete skeleton of an adult woman, Tabun C1.
claims.dating: Revised ESR and new ESR and uranium-series analyses of teeth; the age of 122 ± 16 ka is from a summary, not an abstract we could read.
claims.discovered: Found in the early 1930s in the excavations of Dorothy Garrod and Dorothea Bate.
claims.matters: If this date holds, Neanderthals were in the Levant about as early as the Skhul and Qafzeh modern humans. Simpson et al. 1998 instead dated the skeleton to about 34,000 years.

evidence.text: Simpson et al. dated the jaw by gamma-ray uranium-series to 34 ± 5 ka, younger than layer C, and argued the woman was not a contemporary of the earliest modern humans.

source.citation: Simpson et al. 1998, Journal of Human Evolution

evidence.text: Amos et al. note that the Tabun sequence holds both human types of the Levantine Middle Palaeolithic, usually read as Neanderthals and modern humans.

source.citation: Amos et al. 2025, Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences

evidence.text: Jelinek described a long Tabun sequence from about 130,000 to 50,000 years and argued for continuity there from Neanderthals to modern humans.

claims.claim: 171 retouched clam-shell tools; about a quarter of the shells were gathered live from the sea floor by Neanderthals.
claims.found: 171 retouched tools made on valves of the smooth clam, from 21 layers.
claims.dating: Dated to MIS 5 to early MIS 4; the 130–65 ka span uses standard MIS boundaries, not dates from the paper.
claims.discovered: Excavated in 1949.
claims.matters: Villa et al. infer skin diving and say shell fishing and freshwater fishing were common Neanderthal activities.

evidence.text: Zilhão et al. report large shell middens of Last Interglacial Neanderthals at Figueira Brava on Portugal’s Atlantic coast.

claims.claim: A Neanderthal brow fragment dredged from the North Sea floor, with Late Pleistocene fauna and Middle Palaeolithic tools.

source.citation: Hublin et al. 2009, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: Part of a frontal bone, with small handaxes and Levallois flakes, 15 km off the coast.
claims.dating: Not directly dated; the span reflects the Late Pleistocene fauna and Middle Palaeolithic tools in the same sediments.
claims.discovered: Found in 2001 in sediment dredged from the sea bottom.
claims.matters: Hublin et al. report the first Pleistocene hominin found under the sea and the first in the Netherlands, with isotopes showing a meat-rich diet.

evidence.text: Niekus et al. report a birch-tar-backed flint tool, about 50,000 years old, from the Dutch North Sea, linked to Middle Palaeolithic tools and a Neanderthal fossil.

claims.claim: 23 Neanderthal remains, including the BD 1 jaw with all 16 teeth, from a warm period 127,000 to 116,000 years ago.
claims.found: 23 human remains, all attributed to Neanderthals, among them the well-preserved BD 1 mandible of a young adult.
claims.dating: Geochronological and palaeontological data place the remains in the last interglacial (OIS 5e), 127–116 ka.
claims.matters: Zanolli et al. found the inner structure of the teeth typically Neanderthal and clearly distinct from modern humans.

claims.claim: Butchered bones of at least six Neanderthals, read as cannibalism, about 100,000 years old; later work places the layer in the Last Interglacial.
claims.found: Parts of six Neanderthals with stone-tool marks, mixed with butchered animal bones in the same layer.
claims.dating: Defleur et al. put occupation at about 100,000 years ago; Richards et al. (2024) describe the layers as Last Interglacial (MIS 5e).
claims.discovered: Excavated from 1991.
claims.matters: Defleur et al. infer cannibalism from matching cut marks and bone treatment on humans and animals. The date of the layer is given differently in later work.

evidence.text: Richards et al. describe mandibles from MIS 5e deposits here and link them most closely with Sima de los Huesos and early Neanderthals.

source.citation: Richards et al. 2024, The Anatomical Record

evidence.text: Rougier et al. report butchered Neanderthal bones at Goyet, Belgium, as clear evidence of cannibalism in northern Europe too.

claims.claim: Lake deposits about 125,000 years old where Last Interglacial Neanderthals hunted and butchered straight-tusked elephants weighing up to 13 tonnes.
claims.found: The largest known assemblage of straight-tusked elephants, with butchery marks, in ancient lake deposits.
claims.dating: Lake deposits of the Last Interglacial, about 125,000 years old.
claims.matters: Gaudzinski-Windheuser et al. argue that elephant hunting went on for over 2,000 years and that the meat yields imply Neanderthals were less mobile and lived in larger groups than usually thought.

evidence.text: Kindler et al. describe a ‘fat factory’ at Neumark-Nord where Neanderthals processed at least 172 large mammals for bone grease, a practice once thought to begin only in the Upper Palaeolithic.
Roebroeks et al. report that the Neumark-Nord lake sites suggest landscape modification by hunter-gatherers 125,000 years ago.
Armaroli et al. studied elephant teeth from the site, where over 70 individuals were gathered by Neanderthal hunting, and traced the elephants’ seasonal movements with strontium isotopes.

claims.question: east-asia
claims.claim: Forty-seven fully modern human teeth, dated to 80,000–120,000 years ago.
claims.found: Forty-seven human teeth of entirely modern form, with extinct animals.
claims.dating: Uranium-series dating of flowstone over the layer (minimum 80,000) and of an animal tooth below (maximum 120,000).
claims.discovered: Excavated in 2011–2013 by a team led by Liu Wu.
claims.matters: If right, our species was in southern China long before 50,000 years ago; Sun et al. (2021) date the teeth to the Holocene.

evidence.text: Sun et al. re-dated early modern human fossils from five southern Chinese caves, including Fuyan, with ancient DNA and several methods; they were much younger, some Holocene.

claims.claim: A Neanderthal femur, about 120,000 years old, whose mitochondrial DNA is the deepest-splitting Neanderthal lineage known.
claims.found: An archaic femur from the cave, from which the complete mitochondrial genome was sequenced.
claims.dating: Its age of about 120,000 years comes from genetic analysis, as reported by Peyrégne et al. 2019.
claims.matters: Posth et al. found that its mtDNA split from other Neanderthals about 270,000 years ago. They use it to set a lower time limit for a proposed gene flow from Africa into Neanderthals.

evidence.text: Peyrégne et al. recovered nuclear DNA from this femur and from Scladina, two individuals about 120,000 years old, and found 80,000 years of genetic continuity in European Neanderthals.
Picin et al. found the Stajnia S5000 mtDNA from Poland more distant from the near-contemporary Hohlenstein-Stadel and Scladina Neanderthals than from Mezmaiskaya 1.

claims.claim: The last known Homo erectus, at Ngandong on Java, 108,000 to 117,000 years ago.
claims.found: Twelve skull caps and two shin bones of Homo erectus in a river bone bed.
claims.dating: Bayesian model of 52 dates: uranium-series, luminescence, argon–argon and ESR on the terrace and its fossils.
claims.discovered: Excavated in 1931–1933 by the Dutch Geological Survey; re-excavated from 2008.
claims.matters: Homo erectus lasted on Java about a million years after it first appeared there, perhaps until just before our species arrived.

evidence.text: Swisher et al. ESR and uranium-series dated bovid teeth from the hominin levels to 53,000–27,000 years ago, far younger than this claim.
Indriati et al. argon-dated the terrace to about 546,000 years and got ESR/uranium-series ages up to 143,000; they placed the hominins between the two, older than accepted.

claims.claim: Early Homo sapiens on the Cape coast, about 90,000 to 115,000 years ago.

source.citation: Grine et al. 2017, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: About 50 fragments of skulls, jaws and teeth, many from one horizon, with shellfish and stone tools.
claims.dating: From the site’s stratigraphy and its luminescence, ESR and uranium-series dates, reviewed by Grine et al.
claims.discovered: Excavated in 1967–1968 by Ronald Singer and John Wymer; later by Hilary Deacon and Sarah Wurz.
claims.matters: Some of the earliest Homo sapiens of southern Africa, living on the coast and eating shellfish; some bones bear cut marks.

evidence.text: Wurz et al. dated cave formations by uranium–thorium and placed shell-midden layers at the main site at over 110,000 years, showing steady use of the coast by then.

source.citation: Wurz et al. 2022, Frontiers in Earth Science

claims.question: neanderthal-symbols
claims.claim: Perforated and pigment-stained marine shells, U–Th dated to about 115,000 years ago, long before modern humans reached Europe.
claims.found: Perforated cockle and dog-cockle shells, lumps of yellow and red colourant, and a Spondylus shell holding a red pigment mix.
claims.dating: U–Th dating of the archaeological deposits, as reported by Hoffmann et al. (2018).
claims.matters: Zilhão et al. and Hoffmann et al. read the shells as body ornaments and evidence of Neanderthal symbolism. Earlier work had dated them to about 50,000 years ago.

evidence.text: Zilhão et al. described the perforated valves and the pigment mix of lepidocrocite, hematite and pyrite inside a Spondylus shell, first dated to about 50,000 years ago.
Peresani et al. report a fossil shell coated with hematite from Fumane Cave, Italy, which they suggest was hung as a pendant by Neanderthals.

claims.claim: An open-air site in an arctic setting where Neanderthals hunted reindeer in autumn, with the northernmost Neanderthal remains, from the earlier last glacial.

source.citation: Gaudzinski & Roebroeks 2000, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: Reindeer bones with butchery and marrow breakage, rare Middle Palaeolithic bone tools and Neanderthal remains.
claims.dating: Placed in the earlier last glacial (MIS 5–3) by Gaudzinski & Roebroeks; Ruebens et al.’s radiocarbon dates show it is older than 51,000 years.
claims.discovered: Excavated in 1952; more material was recovered in 1977.
claims.matters: Gaudzinski & Roebroeks read the bones as routine hunting that targeted prime adults. Munson & Marean questioned that ‘prime-dominated’ reading.

evidence.text: Ruebens et al. found that all radiocarbon dates on bone are at or beyond the method’s limit, older than 51,000 years, and that cut marks are common while carnivore marks are rare.

source.citation: Ruebens et al. 2023, Journal of Quaternary Science

evidence.text: Munson & Marean reconsidered whether the Salzgitter-Lebenstedt reindeer show ‘prime-dominated’ hunting, as their title asks: ‘Adults only?’.

source.citation: Munson & Marean 2003, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: A long late Neanderthal sequence, from about 115,000 to 45,000 years ago, where fire use grew over time and flint was probably heat-treated.
claims.found: Over 2,000 flint artefacts studied for burning; possibly heat-treated pieces are commonest among side scrapers.
claims.dating: Lower Mousterian layers about 115,000–70,000 years old; the Micoquian G-layer complex about 60,000–45,000 years old, as reported by Agam et al.
claims.matters: Agam et al. suggest late Neanderthals here deliberately heated flint for some tools, a technique often linked with later humans; they mark the pieces as ‘possibly’ heated.

evidence.text: Delpiano & Uthmeier studied backed knives from the G-layer complex, which mixes Keilmesser and Mousterian traits, and linked them to mobile Neanderthal groups in cold stages.

claims.claim: Shell middens of molluscs, crabs and fish left by Last Interglacial Neanderthals, who also gathered stone pine nuts.
claims.found: Shell middens rich in molluscs, crabs and fish, with land animals and stone pine nuts.
claims.dating: Placed in the Last Interglacial by Zilhão et al.; the 106–86 ka span shown here is approximate.
claims.matters: Zilhão et al. say Atlantic Iberian Neanderthals used the sea on a scale like Middle Stone Age people in southern Africa.

evidence.text: Villa et al. found that Neanderthals at Grotta dei Moscerini, Italy, gathered some clam shells live from the sea floor, likely by diving.
Cortés-Sánchez et al. report shellfish collecting at Bajondillo cave, Spain, across Middle Palaeolithic levels.

source.citation: Cortés-Sánchez et al. 2019, Quaternary Science Reviews

claims.claim: An upper first molar, Pes-3, about 102,000 years old: the first Neanderthal fossil from Serbia and the Central Balkans.

source.citation: Radović et al. 2019, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: A well-preserved right upper first molar with Mousterian tools in layer 4b.
claims.dating: Layer 4b has an estimated age of 102,400 ± 3,200 years, as reported by Radović et al.
claims.matters: Radović et al. note that Neanderthal fossils were known around the Central Balkans but not from it; the tooth’s crown, roots and enamel match Neanderthal patterns.

evidence.text: Majkić et al. studied a cave bear bone with sequential incisions from the Middle Palaeolithic of Pešturina.

source.citation: Majkić et al. 2017, Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory

claims.claim: The bones of Homo floresiensis are 60,000 to 100,000 years old, not as young as first reported.
claims.found: LB1, a near-complete skeleton about 1.1 m tall, and bones of other individuals; their tools span 190,000 to 50,000 years.
claims.dating: Luminescence, uranium-series, argon–argon and radiocarbon dating of the restudied stratigraphy.
claims.discovered: LB1 found in 2003 by an Indonesian–Australian team; named in 2004.
claims.matters: Once dated as late as 12,000 years ago; the new dates leave open whether it met our species. Its ancestry is disputed: dwarfed erectus or an older lineage.

evidence.text: Morwood et al. first dated Homo floresiensis at Liang Bua to before 38,000 until at least 18,000 years ago; the restudy behind this claim revised those ages.
Argue et al. ran phylogenetic analyses and found Homo floresiensis an early Homo lineage, rejecting a close relation to Homo erectus or Homo sapiens.

source.citation: Argue et al. 2017, Journal of Human Evolution

evidence.text: Jacob et al. argued that LB1 falls within modern human variation and was a pygmy Homo sapiens with abnormal growth, including microcephaly.

claims.claim: Neanderthal teeth and bones of at least eight individuals from a cave dated between about 100,000 and more than 39,000 years ago.

source.citation: Harvati et al. 2013, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: Ten isolated teeth, a skull fragment and three other bones, from at least eight people including two children, with Mousterian tools.
claims.dating: The site is dated to between about 100,000 and more than 39,000 years BP, as reported by Harvati et al.
claims.discovered: Excavated from 1993 to 2006 by a Greek–French team.
claims.matters: With Lakonis and Apidima, Harvati et al. see Kalamakia as evidence of a strong Neanderthal presence in the Mani during the Late Pleistocene. Some bones carry carnivore and human marks.

evidence.text: Kolendrianou et al. studied small mammals, teeth wear and lithics, and found Neanderthals came to the cave in short and longer stays, using poor local stone carefully.
Bartsiokas et al. call the Lakonis and Kalamakia specimens nearby younger Neanderthals than Apidima 2.

source.citation: Bartsiokas et al. 2017, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: The Teshik-Tash child, found in 1938, long the easternmost Neanderthal; its status was argued until DNA and new shape analyses.

source.citation: Gunz & Bulygina 2012, American Journal of Physical Anthropology

claims.found: The skull and other bones of a child, with Mousterian stone tools.
claims.dating: No reliable numerical age in the sources checked; it comes from Mousterian layers. The range shown is approximate.
claims.discovered: Excavated in 1938 by Alexey Okladnikov.
claims.matters: Gunz & Bulygina 2012 place it firmly among Neanderthals; Glantz et al. 2008 found its measurements equivocal.

source.citation: Glantz et al. 2008, American Journal of Physical Anthropology

evidence.text: Glantz et al. found problems with the old reconstruction; the skull grouped with Upper Palaeolithic modern humans and the jaw with recent humans in some analyses.

source.citation: Glantz et al. 2008, American Journal of Physical Anthropology

evidence.text: Krause et al. found that mitochondrial DNA from remains in Uzbekistan and the Altai falls within European Neanderthal variation, extending their range 2,000 km east.
Andreeva et al. note its control region carries variants of two haplogroups and question the sequence.

claims.claim: Burials of early modern humans, about 92,000 years old.
claims.found: Skeletons of more than a dozen early modern humans, several buried, one child with deer antlers, with Middle Palaeolithic tools
claims.dating: Thermoluminescence of burnt flints from the burial layers, about 92,000 years
claims.discovered: First dug in the 1930s by René Neuville and Moshe Stekelis; most burials found 1965–1979 by Bernard Vandermeersch
claims.matters: Among the oldest known burials. The date showed modern humans in the Levant before many Neanderthals there, overturning the view that Neanderthals were their ancestors.

evidence.text: McDermott et al. dated tooth fragments by uranium-series and, with ESR ages, found Qafzeh’s early modern humans about 100,000 ± 5,000 years old.
Hovers et al. studied ochre from the 92,000-year-old Qafzeh record and found it was chosen for its colour, which they read as a sign of symbolic culture.

claims.question: east-asia
claims.claim: Homo sapiens in Laos by 68,000 to 86,000 years ago.
claims.found: A frontal bone (TPL 6) and a shin fragment (TPL 7) from the deepest layers, below earlier finds.
claims.dating: Bayesian model of luminescence dates on sediment and uranium-series and ESR on animal teeth.
claims.discovered: First skull found in 2009 by a Lao–French–American team; TPL 6 and TPL 7 found later.
claims.matters: It supports an early dispersal of our species into Southeast Asia, well before 50,000 years ago.

evidence.text: Demeter et al. described the first modern human skull from Tam Pa Ling, with a minimum age of 51,000–46,000 years and a maximum of about 63,000 from direct uranium dating.
Demeter et al. described a second individual, a jaw with a chin but some archaic traits, showing wide variation among early modern humans in the region.

claims.claim: A Neanderthal molar from a Micoquian layer whose mitochondrial DNA dates to MIS 5a, the oldest Neanderthal specimen from Central-Eastern Europe.
claims.found: Neanderthal teeth from Micoquian layers, including molar S5000, which gave a mitochondrial genome.
claims.dating: The S5000 mtDNA dates to MIS 5a (roughly 82,000–71,000 years ago), per Picin et al.; layer dates from bone and teeth are older than 49,000.
claims.discovered: The teeth were found in 2008.
claims.matters: Picin et al. found the S5000 mtDNA closest to Mezmaiskaya 1 in the Caucasus. With shared Micoquian tools, they argue for Neanderthal movement between Poland and the North Caucasus.

evidence.text: Dąbrowski et al. identified a second tooth from the same layer, S4300, as a Neanderthal lower molar from another individual.
Andreeva et al. found Mezmaiskaya 3 closest to Mezmaiskaya 1 and Stajnia S5000.
Slimak et al. note that molecular ages for Stajnia S5000 disagree with its layer dates.

claims.claim: Two lumps of birch tar made by Neanderthals, from a layer the geology places at more than 80,000 years old.

source.citation: Koller et al. 2001, European Journal of Archaeology

claims.found: Two pieces of birch pitch; one carries a fingerprint and the imprints of a flint tool and of wood, as if it fixed a haft.
claims.dating: From a lignite-mine layer whose geological age was put at older than 80,000 years.
claims.discovered: Found in 1963 in an opencast lignite mine north of the Harz.
claims.matters: Birch tar is the oldest known synthetic material. Whether making it needed advanced planning is argued: Kozowyk et al. showed simple methods work, while Schmidt et al. argue the Königsaue tar was made a harder way.

evidence.text: Schmidt et al. compared the Königsaue tar with experimental tars and concluded it was distilled in an underground, low-oxygen set-up, not by the simplest method, which they read as cumulative culture.

source.citation: Schmidt et al. 2023, Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences

evidence.text: Kozowyk et al. made useful amounts of tar with simple methods and materials Neanderthals already used, and argue that precise temperature control was not needed.

claims.claim: OR-1, a child’s teeth and skull fragments from Middle Palaeolithic layers, with teeth judged essentially Neanderthal.

source.citation: Bailey et al. 2008, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: Part of the upper teeth and a fragmentary skull of one juvenile, OR-1.
claims.dating: Plisson et al. give about 80,000 years for the oldest layers, in 10 m of deposits covering 40,000 years; OR-1’s exact age is not given here.
claims.discovered: Recovered in 2003 by an Uzbek–American team.
claims.matters: Bailey et al. find the teeth Neanderthal; Glantz et al. 2008 call the skull more ambiguous, so its species is still debated.

evidence.text: Glantz et al. describe a fairly Neanderthal-like set of teeth but more ambiguous skull anatomy.

source.citation: Glantz et al. 2008, Journal of Human Evolution

evidence.text: Plisson et al. report possible light weapon tips in the oldest layers, about 80,000 years old, a trait so far known from modern human sites.

claims.claim: The Border Cave 5 jaw, about 74,000 years old.

source.citation: Grün et al. 2003, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: The lower jaw of an adult modern human; the cave also holds an infant burial with a shell ornament.
claims.dating: ESR on a fragment of tooth enamel with laser-ablation uranium profiling: 74 ± 5 thousand years.
claims.discovered: Found in 1974 in Peter Beaumont’s excavation.
claims.matters: It answers a claim that the jaw was Iron Age, confirming modern humans in the cave in the Middle Stone Age.

evidence.text: Millard re-analysed Border Cave’s ESR dates with Bayesian statistics and placed the BC5 jaw at 72,000–61,000 years (95% range).

claims.claim: Ochre engraved with cross-hatching, about 77,000 years old.
claims.found: Two pieces of red ochre engraved with abstract patterns; also shell beads and bone tools.
claims.dating: Thermoluminescence of burnt stone tools (mean 77,000) and OSL of an overlying dune (70,000).
claims.discovered: Excavated from 1991 by Christopher Henshilwood; the engraved ochres found in 1999–2000.
claims.matters: Evidence of symbolic thought in Africa at least 35,000 years before the Upper Palaeolithic of Europe.

evidence.text: Jacobs et al. dated single quartz grains by optical luminescence and placed the last Middle Stone Age phase, with the engraved ochre, at 72,700 ± 3,100 years.

source.citation: Jacobs et al. 2006, Journal of Human Evolution

evidence.text: Tribolo et al. dated five burnt stone tools from the Still Bay layers by thermoluminescence to 74,000 ± 5,000 years, in line with ESR and OSL dates.
Henshilwood et al. reported 13 more engraved ochre pieces from levels about 100,000–75,000 years old, suggesting a long tradition of symbolic marking.

source.citation: Henshilwood et al. 2009, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: Neanderthals hunted red deer, ibex and bison in warm seasons and cut meat from golden eagles, a raven, a wolf and a lynx.
claims.found: Animal bones from Mousterian levels, almost all herbivores, plus cut-marked bird and carnivore bones.
claims.dating: Level D sits at the MIS 5–4 transition (about 71 ka); the 75–67 ka span here is approximate, not a date from the paper.
claims.matters: Uzunidis et al. reconstruct a seasonal hunting round. Gómez-Olivencia et al. give the first evidence of bird and carnivore use in the Cantabrian region.

evidence.text: Gómez-Olivencia et al. found cut marks on two golden eagles, a raven, a wolf and a lynx from the Mousterian levels of Axlor.

claims.question: australia
claims.claim: Stone tools and pigments of people in northern Australia by about 65,000 years ago.
claims.found: Stone tools, ground-edge axe heads, grindstones and ground ochre in the lowest dense layer of a rock shelter
claims.dating: Optically stimulated luminescence of single sand grains, with radiocarbon of charcoal in the upper layers
claims.discovered: Dug in 1973 and 1989; re-excavated 2012 and 2015 by a team led by Chris Clarkson, with the Mirarr traditional owners
claims.matters: Clarkson et al. read it as people in Australia by about 65,000 years ago. Others, e.g. O’Connell et al. 2018, argue the tools may have moved down in the sand and favour arrival 47,000–50,000 years ago.

evidence.text: O’Connell et al. reviewed the evidence from South China to Sahul and judged an age of more than 50,000 years for Madjedbebe unlikely to be valid.
Florin et al. found charred plant foods, some needing processing, in Madjedbebe layers dated to 65,000–53,000 years.

claims.claim: A layer full of horned skulls of large herbivores, brought in by Neanderthals and read as a symbolic accumulation.

source.citation: Baquedano et al. 2023, Nature Human Behaviour

claims.found: Mostly crania of large ungulates with cut and percussion marks, small hearths and Mousterian tools in Level 3.
claims.dating: Biochronology and dating place Level 3 in MIS 4 or the first half of MIS 3; the 71–43 ka span is approximate.
claims.matters: Baquedano et al. see no food purpose for keeping the skulls and suggest symbolic intent. Villaescusa et al. (2026) studied how the layer formed.

evidence.text: Villaescusa et al. found limited movement of material after burial and distinct formation patterns for the crania and the rockfall that holds them.

source.citation: Villaescusa et al. 2026, Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences

claims.claim: Shanidar Z, a Neanderthal found by the ‘flower burial’, preliminarily dated to 60,000–70,000 years ago.
claims.found: The articulated upper body of an adult, near remains of at least ten Neanderthals found in the 1950s.
claims.dating: Preliminary OSL dating of the sediments, by Oxford; reported as in progress.
claims.discovered: Earlier remains found 1953–1960 by Ralph Solecki; Shanidar Z in 2018 by a team led by Graeme Barker.
claims.matters: Solecki argued Neanderthals buried their dead here with flowers; the flowers are disputed, and the new find is read as an intentional burial.

evidence.text: Solecki reported clusters of flower pollen in the grave of Shanidar IV and read them as a flower burial.
Hunt et al. reviewed the pollen evidence and found that at least some clumps were probably left by nesting solitary bees, though the bodies were deliberately placed.

source.citation: Hunt et al. 2023, Journal of Archaeological Science

evidence.text: Sommer re-evaluated the Shanidar IV ‘flower burial’ as evidence of Neanderthal burial ritual (title seen only).
López-Polín et al. describe Shanidar Z as about 75,000 years old, older than the preliminary 60,000–70,000 years first reported.
Pomeroy et al. found bones in 2015–16 beside the spot where Shanidar 5 lay in 1960 and assign them to that man, aged 40–50 at death.

source.citation: Pomeroy et al. 2017, Journal of Human Evolution

evidence.text: Henry et al. found plant remains in the tartar of Shanidar III’s teeth, including date palm, legumes and grass seeds, some of them cooked.
Trinkaus and Villotte found bony growths in Shanidar 1’s ear canals that point to hearing loss, adding to his other injuries; they read his survival as a sign of social support.

claims.claim: Two Neanderthal children, each about two years old, buried in pits in the Mousterian layers of Dederiyeh Cave.
claims.found: Two child skeletons: one found in 1993 lying on its back, arms out and legs bent; a second in a dug pit, with the first facial bones from Syria.
claims.dating: No numerical age in the abstracts checked; the layers hold Tabun B-type Mousterian tools, of the late Middle Palaeolithic. The range shown is approximate.
claims.discovered: Found in 1993 and 1997–98 by a Japanese–Syrian team led by Takeru Akazawa and Sultan Muhesen.
claims.matters: Akazawa et al. read the posture of the first child as an intentional burial and link Neanderthals to the Tabun B-type industry.

evidence.text: Akazawa et al. found the second child in a pit dug into a Mousterian layer, sharing many traits with the first.
Griggo found only humans built up the cave’s bones: Neanderthals hunted goats, deer and gazelle and carried them whole into the cave, and seem to have scavenged aurochs and rhino.
Zollikofer et al. rebuilt the near-complete Dederiyeh pelvis and found Neanderthal and human pelves differ in shape from an early age.

claims.question: neanderthal-burial

claims.claim: A Neanderthal molar from Shukbah Cave, the southernmost known Neanderthal fossil, found with Nubian Levallois tools.
claims.found: A lower first molar with clear Neanderthal traits, with Levallois stone tools including Nubian points and cores.
claims.dating: Not dated directly; Blinkhorn et al. place it in the period, about 70,000–50,000 years ago, when Neanderthals spread into the Levant. Range approximate.
claims.discovered: Dug by Dorothy Garrod in 1928; the tooth and tools were re-examined in 2021.
claims.matters: Blinkhorn et al. 2021 say Nubian Levallois tools are not a marker of Homo sapiens alone; Hallinan et al. 2022 dispute the link at Shukbah.

evidence.text: Hallinan et al. argue there is no direct evidence for Nubian Levallois technology, or for its link to Neanderthals, at Shukbah.
Blinkhorn et al. replied that treating Nubian Levallois as a unique marker of Homo sapiens rests on weak foundations.

claims.claim: The first Neanderthal remains from an open-air site in the Levant, visited repeatedly 60,000–70,000 years ago.
claims.found: A skull fragment, an upper third molar and the leg bones of a young Neanderthal man, from intact layers.
claims.dating: Optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) ages of 70,000–60,000 years.
claims.discovered: Excavated at an open-air site in northern Israel; reported by Been et al. in 2017.
claims.matters: Been et al. say Neanderthals also used open landscapes, not only caves, and were a resilient Levantine population shortly before Homo sapiens arrived.

evidence.text: Blinkhorn et al. say Neanderthals expanded south into the Levant between about 70,000 and 50,000 years ago, after earlier Homo sapiens.

claims.claim: Wezmeh 1, the unerupted premolar of a child aged about eight, shown by its inner structure to be Neanderthal.

source.citation: Zanolli et al. 2019, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: One upper premolar from a child of about 8 ± 2 years, in a fauna rich in carnivores.
claims.dating: Uranium-series dating of the animal bones gives 70,000 to 11,000 years; the tooth itself is not dated.
claims.discovered: Reassessed with micro-CT by Zanolli et al. in 2019.
claims.matters: Zanolli et al. call it the first direct evidence of Neanderthals on the western edge of the Iranian Plateau.

evidence.text: Heydari-Guran et al. later reported a Neanderthal milk canine from Bawa Yawan, in the same region.

claims.claim: A human forearm bone from the Mousterian levels of Bisitun Cave, closest in size to Neanderthals.
claims.found: The upper shaft of a right radius; a second ‘human’ tooth turned out to be a bovid incisor.
claims.dating: No numerical age in the abstract; it comes from Mousterian levels. The range shown is approximate.
claims.discovered: Identified as human in 1949 by Carleton Coon; restudied by Trinkaus and Biglari in 2006.
claims.matters: Trinkaus & Biglari find it near Neanderthals and Upper Palaeolithic modern humans, but unlike other Middle Palaeolithic fossils of south-west Asia.

evidence.text: Heydari-Guran et al. report a Neanderthal milk canine with Zagros Mousterian tools at Bawa Yawan, also near Kermanshah.

claims.claim: Homo luzonensis, a new species named from Callao Cave, with minimum ages of 50,000 and 67,000 years.
claims.found: Teeth, finger and toe bones and a thigh fragment from at least three individuals.
claims.dating: Uranium-series dating directly on a foot bone and a tooth, giving minimum ages.
claims.discovered: The foot bone found in 2007 by Armand Mijares’s team; further remains in 2011 and 2015.
claims.matters: A second small-bodied island species east of the Wallace Line, with a mix of primitive and derived traits.

evidence.text: Mijares et al. first reported a Homo foot bone from Callao Cave, directly dated by uranium-series to a minimum of 66,700 ± 1,000 years.

source.citation: Mijares et al. 2010, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: Forty Neanderthal bones collected by hyenas, 66,000 to 65,000 years ago, in the cave that gave a famous skull in 1939.

source.citation: Rolfo et al. 2023, Quaternary Science Reviews

claims.found: Large mammal bones, 40 of them Neanderthal including large parts of skulls, in inner deposits.
claims.dating: U/Th dating of speleothems constrains the accumulation to 66–65 ka.
claims.discovered: The cave and its skull were found in 1939; new excavations began about eight decades later.
claims.matters: Rolfo et al. say spotted hyenas gathered the bones at a time when people rarely or never used the cave.

claims.question: neanderthal-symbols
claims.claim: Red paintings under carbonate crusts U–Th dated to more than 64,000 years ago, which would make them Neanderthal; disputed.
claims.found: Red paintings, including linear signs, with carbonate crusts that formed on top of the paint.
claims.dating: U–Th dating of carbonate crusts over the paint gives minimum ages; Hoffmann et al. report over 64,000 years for the three caves.
claims.matters: Hoffmann et al. say the paintings predate modern humans in Europe by at least 20,000 years, so Neanderthals made them. Slimak et al. and Aubert et al. question the dates.

evidence.text: Slimak et al. re-read the geochronological data and say they better support an age of about 47,000 years for the paintings.
Hoffmann et al. replied that the criticisms of their oldest U–Th dates, on open-system behaviour and detrital thorium, are unfounded.
Aubert et al. argue that the early dates for ‘Neanderthal cave art’ in Spain may be wrong.

source.citation: Aubert et al. 2018, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.question: neanderthal-symbols
claims.claim: Paintings under carbonate crusts U–Th dated to more than 64,000 years ago, which would make them Neanderthal; disputed.
claims.found: Paintings on the cave walls, partly covered by carbonate crusts; art in the three caves includes hand stencils, signs and animals.
claims.dating: U–Th dating of carbonate crusts over the paint; Hoffmann et al. report minimum ages older than 64,000 years for the three caves.
claims.matters: One of three Spanish caves Hoffmann et al. used to argue that Neanderthals made cave art. The dating method and its results are contested.

evidence.text: Slimak et al. re-read the geochronological data and say they better support an age of about 47,000 years for the paintings.
Hoffmann et al. replied that the criticisms of their oldest U–Th dates, on open-system behaviour and detrital thorium, are unfounded.
Aubert et al. argue that the early dates for ‘Neanderthal cave art’ in Spain may be wrong.

source.citation: Aubert et al. 2018, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.question: neanderthal-symbols
claims.claim: Red paint on a large stalagmite curtain under crusts U–Th dated to more than 64,000 years ago, which would make it Neanderthal; disputed.
claims.found: Red pigment on a large speleothem curtain, partly covered by carbonate crusts.
claims.dating: U–Th dating of crusts over the paint gives minimum ages older than 64,000 years (Hoffmann et al. 2018).
claims.matters: Pitarch Martí et al. (2021) confirmed the paint was applied by people and did not come from colourant sources inside the cave. The dates and their Neanderthal attribution are contested.

evidence.text: Pitarch Martí et al. found the Ardales paint human-made, not from colourant outcrops in the cave, and varying in make-up with age, suggesting use over a long time.
Slimak et al. re-read the geochronological data and say they better support an age of about 47,000 years for the paintings.
Hoffmann et al. replied that the criticisms of their oldest U–Th dates, on open-system behaviour and detrital thorium, are unfounded.

claims.question: neanderthal-symbols
claims.claim: Non-figurative finger marks on the cave wall, made before the cave was sealed more than 57,000 ± 3,000 years ago.
claims.found: Spatially organised, non-figurative marks on the cave wall, with only Mousterian stone tools inside the cave.
claims.dating: 50 OSL ages on sediment that sealed the cave give a minimum age of 57 ± 3 ka for the marks.
claims.discovered: Found in the 19th century; first dug in the early 20th century.
claims.matters: Marquet et al. call these the earliest unambiguous Neanderthal engravings, made before Homo sapiens reached the region. The same site gave a disputed stone ‘mask’.

evidence.text: Marquet & Lorblanchet argued that a worked stone from a Mousterian layer here, pierced by a bone splinter, was meant to look like a face.

claims.question: neanderthal-symbols
claims.claim: A perforated cave bear femur from Neanderthal levels that Turk et al. read as a musical instrument; others see holes made by carnivores.
claims.found: The femur of a young cave bear with several holes, from a Mousterian layer.
claims.dating: Placed in Mousterian levels; the often-quoted age of about 50,000–60,000 years is from ESR work not checked here.
claims.discovered: Found in 1995.
claims.matters: If made by people, Turk et al. argue it shows Neanderthal music. Morley and Diedrich see no need for human agency, putting the holes down to carnivores. Turk et al. 2020 say experts remain divided.

evidence.text: Morley reviewed the research and concluded there is no need to invoke hominin agency to explain the features of the bone.
Diedrich argued that punctured cave bear cub femora like this are not instruments but bones bitten by Ice Age spotted hyenas.
Turk et al. reviewed the debate and say it splits experts, and could be settled only by similar finds in comparable, well-dated contexts.

claims.claim: Kebara 2, a buried Neanderthal man, in deposits dated by thermoluminescence to about 48,000–60,000 years ago.
claims.found: The buried Kebara 2 skeleton, with the most intact Neanderthal pelvis yet found and a rare hyoid (throat) bone.
claims.dating: Thermoluminescence of 38 burnt flints from 4 m of deposits: about 60,000 to 48,000 years.
claims.discovered: Found in the 1982–90 excavations led by Ofer Bar-Yosef and Bernard Vandermeersch.
claims.matters: Valladas et al. 1987 placed Neanderthals in the Levant late in the Middle Palaeolithic. Whether the hyoid shows Neanderthals could speak is still argued.

evidence.text: Arensburg et al. found the Kebara hyoid almost identical to ours and concluded the anatomy for speech was fully developed by the Middle Palaeolithic.
D’Anastasio et al. found the inner structure of the hyoid also like ours, which they say is consistent with a capacity for speech; they note the question remains controversial.
Rak and Arensburg dated the skeleton to about 50,000–55,000 years and found its pelvic inlet as large as a modern human’s, despite a very long pubic bone.

source.citation: Rak & Arensburg 1987, American Journal of Physical Anthropology

evidence.text: Bar-Yosef et al. summarised the 1982–90 dig: a complex stratigraphy, hearths, ash lenses and concentrations of bones and tools.

claims.claim: Neanderthals at Chagyrskaya Cave 49,000–59,000 years ago: 74 remains, Micoquian-like tools and a high-coverage genome.
claims.found: 74 Neanderthal remains and about 90,000 stone tools; the people hunted bison on a dry steppe.
claims.dating: Age range of 59,000 to 49,000 years at 95.4% probability, from the deposits.
claims.discovered: Excavated by Novosibirsk teams; Kolobova et al. reported the assemblage in 2020.
claims.matters: Kolobova et al. trace the tools to central and eastern Europe, 3,000 km west, and see two or more Neanderthal arrivals in the Altai.
