evidence.text: Mafessoni et al. sequenced a female from the cave to 27-fold coverage; she was closer to western Neanderthals than to earlier ones at Denisova Cave.
Skov et al. found a father and daughter among 11 people from the cave, and low Y diversity best explained by women moving between communities.
Zubova et al. read a hollow drilled into a molar, Chagyrskaya 64, as treatment of tooth decay with a stone tool, about 59,000 years ago.
Slon et al. found Neanderthal mtDNA in Chagyrskaya sediments.

claims.claim: Neanderthal remains at least 44,000 years old, with DNA from two people, close in time to the Chagyrskaya group.
claims.found: Neanderthal teeth and bones with Sibiryachikha-type stone tools; two people gave DNA.
claims.dating: Single-amino-acid radiocarbon on three Neanderthal bones: at least 44,000 years, as the paper gives them. Upper bound approximate.
claims.discovered: Mitochondrial DNA first reported by Krause et al. 2007; genome-wide data for two people by Skov et al. 2022.
claims.matters: Skov et al. find one Okladnikov person with mtDNA identical to a Chagyrskaya Neanderthal, so they lived within a few thousand years of each other.

evidence.text: Krause et al. found the mitochondrial DNA of remains from the Altai and Uzbekistan within European Neanderthal variation.
Kolobova et al. describe layer 3 as a camp where horse and rhino carcasses were butchered and eaten.

source.citation: Kolobova et al. 2025, Archaeology, Ethnology & Anthropology of Eurasia

evidence.text: Skoglund et al. read the complete mtDNA of a contaminated Okladnikov bone.

claims.claim: Neanderthal hand, arm and leg bones and teeth, the youngest about 43,500 calendar years old and others earlier in MIS 3.

source.citation: Trinkaus et al. 2007, American Journal of Physical Anthropology

claims.found: Fragmentary human bones and teeth (Oliveira 1–9); a tibia shows carnivore gnawing.
claims.dating: Oliveira 1–2 date to about 39,000 radiocarbon years BP (about 43,500 cal BP); others come from older MIS 3 layers.
claims.matters: Trinkaus et al. and Willman et al. align the remains with Neanderthals, documenting early MIS 3 Neanderthals in western Iberia.

evidence.text: Willman et al. described five more remains and found the humerus robust or stocky like other Iberian Neanderthals.

source.citation: Willman et al. 2012, American Journal of Physical Anthropology

evidence.text: Angelucci & Zilhão found the 35,000–70,000-year sequence had near-continuous occupation and intact layers in its richer part.
Deschamps & Zilhão used tool refits to show little disturbance in the basal layers, which TL and U-series place in late MIS 5 or early MIS 4.

claims.claim: The ‘Old Man’ of La Chapelle-aux-Saints, about 47,000 to 56,000 years old.
claims.found: A nearly complete skeleton of an older man who had lost most of his teeth, in a pit in the cave floor.
claims.dating: ESR dating of animal teeth from the burial layer.
claims.discovered: Found in 1908 by Amédée and Jean Bouyssonie and Louis Bardon.
claims.matters: Boule’s stooped reconstruction shaped the brutish image of Neanderthals for decades; Rendu et al. (2013) argue the pit was a deliberate burial.

evidence.text: Rendu et al. re-excavated the site and concluded the Neanderthal was laid in a pit dug by others and quickly covered: an intentional burial.
Dibble et al. took a critical look at the evidence offered for an intentional burial at La Chapelle-aux-Saints and questioned it.

source.citation: Dibble et al. 2015, Journal of Archaeological Science

evidence.text: Gargett argued that articulated skeletons are not by themselves proof of deliberate Middle Palaeolithic burial, as natural cave processes can explain them.

claims.question: neanderthal-burial

claims.claim: Amud 7, the most complete Neanderthal infant aged 6 to 14 months, from a cave with Neanderthal remains about 51,000–56,000 years old.
claims.found: Several Neanderthal remains; Amud 7 is an articulated infant skeleton of about 111 pieces found in place.
claims.dating: Been et al. give about 51,000–56,000 years for the Middle Palaeolithic tool assemblages, citing earlier dating studies.
claims.discovered: The cave was dug in the 1960s and the 1990s; Amud 7 was first described in 1994 by Rak, Kimbel and Hovers.
claims.matters: Been et al. 2026 find the infant grew unusually fast, like other rare Neanderthal infants, and read this as a distinct Neanderthal way of growing up.

evidence.text: Hallin et al. used isotopes in goat and gazelle teeth to show Neanderthals at Amud (53–70 ka) lived in wetter conditions than modern humans at nearby Qafzeh (about 92 ka).

source.citation: Hallin et al. 2012, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: A Neanderthal milk tooth with animal bones radiocarbon dated to 46,820 ± 3,290 BP: roughly 55,000–43,200 calendar years ago.

source.citation: Toussaint et al. 2010, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: A child’s lower right second milk molar, with stone tools once seen as transitional.
claims.dating: Radiocarbon on associated animal bone, 46,820 ± 3,290 BP; calibrated with IntCal20 by this site (95%), the range reaching the curve’s limit.
claims.discovered: Found in 1984 at the cave entrance.
claims.matters: Toussaint et al. found the tooth’s shape and enamel consistent with a Neanderthal, settling a long uncertainty.

evidence.text: Devièse et al. date the disappearance of Neanderthals from Northwest Europe to 44,200–40,600 cal BP, after the age given for this tooth.

claims.question: europe
claims.claim: A child’s tooth and tools read as our species, about 54,000 years ago, between Neanderthal layers.
claims.found: A child’s milk tooth read as Homo sapiens, in a layer with small ‘Neronian’ points, between layers with Neanderthal teeth and tools
claims.dating: Luminescence and radiocarbon dating, with layers counted from soot films on the cave wall; the layer is about 56,800–51,700 years old
claims.discovered: Excavated since 1990 by a team led by Ludovic Slimak
claims.matters: Slimak et al. read it as a modern human incursion into Europe about 10,000 years before others known. The reading rests on one tooth and its link to the tools.

claims.claim: A fragment of three-ply cord made of inner bark, found on a stone tool, from a layer dated to about 52,000–41,000 years ago.
claims.found: A 3-ply cord fragment of inner bark fibres on a stone tool, found in place in level 4.2.
claims.dating: ESR and U-series dates for level 4.2 range from 41 ± 2 ka to 52 ± 2 ka, as reported by Hardy et al.
claims.matters: Hardy et al. say twisted cord implies complex multi-part technology and makes the idea of Neanderthal cognitive inferiority hard to hold.

evidence.text: Ruebens et al. found human cut marks across many species in layer 1 at the site, and a point-rich layer 4.1 of MIS 3 age.

source.citation: Ruebens et al. 2022, Journal of Paleolithic Archaeology

evidence.text: Niekus et al. report a 50,000-year-old flint tool with birch tar from the Dutch North Sea, more evidence of Neanderthal multi-part technology.

claims.claim: Late Neanderthals at Pech-de-l’Azé I chose manganese dioxide, which may have helped them make fire; the child’s layer dates to about 51,000–37,000 years ago.
claims.found: Many small black blocks of manganese oxide in Mousterian layers, and the skull and jaw of a Neanderthal child.
claims.dating: Coupled ESR/U-series on 16 animal teeth: layer 6 at 37–51 ka, with radiocarbon on bone at about 41.7–43 ka (Soressi et al. 2007).
claims.matters: Heyes et al. argue manganese dioxide was used to light fires, not only as black pigment. Whether Neanderthals could make fire at will is debated (Dibble et al. 2017).

evidence.text: Soressi et al. placed the Neanderthal child at the base of layer 6, an MTA type B layer, and say this confirms Neanderthals made that industry.

source.citation: Soressi et al. 2007, Journal of Human Evolution

evidence.text: Sorensen et al. found wear on late Mousterian bifaces from several French sites that matches striking pyrite to make fire.
Dibble et al. report that fire evidence in southwest France falls sharply in cold periods and suggest these Neanderthals may not have been able to make fire.
Sandgathe et al. argue that habitual fire use came late and that earlier Neanderthal fire use was sporadic and opportunistic.

claims.question: neanderthal-symbols
claims.claim: A giant deer toe bone engraved with a pattern of lines, at least 51,000 years old, from a context linked to Neanderthals.

source.citation: Leder et al. 2021, Nature Ecology & Evolution

claims.found: An engraved phalanx of a giant deer at the former cave entrance.
claims.dating: At least 51,000 years old, as reported by Leder et al.
claims.matters: Leder et al. argue that composing lines into a design shows conceptual imagination, and that Neanderthals made symbolic expressions before Homo sapiens reached Central Europe. Claims of Neanderthal symbolism are often contested.

evidence.text: Russo et al. report cave lion toe bones at least 190,000 years old from Einhornhöhle, which they read as the earliest use of cave lion skin by Neanderthals in Central Europe.

claims.question: neanderthal-admixture
claims.claim: From ancient and present-day genomes, one long period of mixing, about 43,500 to 50,500 years ago.
claims.wikipedia: Interbreeding between archaic and modern humans
claims.found: No single find: Neanderthal DNA segments in more than 300 genomes, ancient and present-day, spanning the past 50,000 years
claims.dating: Lengths of Neanderthal DNA segments, which shorten each generation, anchored on radiocarbon ages of the ancient people
claims.matters: Iasi et al. find one long period of mixing, about 7,000 years, centred about 47,000 years ago. Sümer et al. 2024 give a close but narrower date; the papers differ on how long it lasted.

evidence.text: Sümer et al. dated the single admixture event shared by all non-Africans to about 49,000–45,000 years ago, from genomes from Ranis and Zlatý kůň.
Sankararaman et al. measured linkage in present-day European genomes and dated the last Neanderthal gene flow to 86,000–37,000 years ago, most likely 65,000–47,000.
Fu et al. found long Neanderthal segments in the 45,000-year-old Ust’-Ishim genome, placing the gene flow 7,000–13,000 years before he lived: somewhat earlier than this range.

claims.question: australia
claims.claim: A review of the sites finds people reached Sahul (Australia and New Guinea joined by low seas) about 47,000 to 50,000 years ago, not earlier.
claims.found: No single find: a review of dated archaeological sites in Southeast Asia, Australia and New Guinea
claims.dating: Re-assesses published radiocarbon and luminescence ages, keeping only those the authors judge reliable
claims.matters: O’Connell et al. argue for arrival about 47,000–50,000 years ago and doubt the older ages, chiefly Madjedbebe’s; Clarkson et al. stand by 65,000 years. The two readings are both shown.

evidence.text: Clarkson et al. reported new excavations at Madjedbebe, with optical dating and artefact refits, and placed the start of human occupation about 65,000 years ago.
Florin et al. found charred plant foods at Madjedbebe in layers dated to 65,000–53,000 years, which they attribute to Australia’s earliest known people.

claims.question: chatelperronian
claims.claim: Neanderthal bones, identified by ancient proteins and DNA, date to the Châtelperronian layers with their ornaments, within 50,000–40,000 years ago; the link is debated.
claims.found: Châtelperronian tools and body ornaments with Neanderthal remains, mainly teeth, plus bone fragments identified as hominin by ZooMS.
claims.dating: Radiocarbon dates on bone and the identified hominin fragments; Hublin et al. (2012) place the Châtelperronian in the 50,000–40,000-year window.
claims.matters: Welker et al. and Hublin et al. say Neanderthals made the Châtelperronian here. Higham et al. (2010) found dates varied enough to suggest mixing of layers, which makes the link uncertain.

evidence.text: Hublin et al. dated 40 bones from the Mousterian, Châtelperronian and Protoaurignacian layers and found the results inconsistent with layer admixture.
Higham et al. obtained 31 radiocarbon dates with an unexpected spread, suggesting some mixing that makes the association of ornaments and human remains hard to trust.
Gravina et al. note that Neanderthal authorship of the Châtelperronian rests on only two sites, this one and Saint-Césaire, and found the Saint-Césaire link unreliable.

claims.question: neanderthal-extinction
claims.claim: Neanderthal fossils once dated to under 42,000 years ago were re-dated to at least 10,000 radiocarbon years older; the late date was a key argument for a southern refuge.
claims.found: Neanderthal fossils with Mousterian tools.
claims.dating: Ultrafiltered radiocarbon on bone gave ages close to or beyond the method’s limit; earlier dates had been under 42 ka cal BP.
claims.matters: Wood et al. argue that the late southern Iberian dates are unreliable. Others, such as Zilhão et al. (2017), still see late Neanderthals in the south.

evidence.text: Zilhão et al. found a Mousterian layer at Cueva Antón no more than 37,100 years old, which they see as support for late Neanderthals in southern Iberia.

claims.question: neanderthal-symbols
claims.claim: An eagle toe bone used as an ornament by Neanderthals in a Châtelperronian layer, the first such find in Iberia.
claims.found: An imperial eagle foot phalanx with marks, from the Châtelperronian layer.
claims.dating: Châtelperronian layer; the 50–40 ka span follows the date window Hublin et al. (2012) give for the Châtelperronian, not a site date.
claims.matters: Rodríguez-Hidalgo et al. see a long Neanderthal tradition of wearing eagle talons, lasting into the last Neanderthal populations.

evidence.text: Finlayson et al. found a link between Neanderthals, raptors and corvids across many Palaearctic sites and at Gibraltar caves, and wing feather removal.
Peresani et al. found cut and scrape marks only on the wings of raptors and other birds at Fumane, Italy, and read this as removal of feathers.

claims.claim: Faecal biomarkers and gut-microbe DNA from Neanderthal occupation floors about 50,000 years old.
claims.found: Sediments from occupation floors containing faecal biomarkers, and ancient microbial DNA.
claims.dating: The site’s unit X dates to about 50,000 years ago, as given by Sistiaga et al. and Rampelli et al.
claims.matters: Sistiaga et al. read the biomarkers as a mostly meat diet with real plant intake: the oldest identified human faeces.

evidence.text: Rampelli et al. found gut bacteria known from modern humans, such as Blautia and Bifidobacterium, only in the Neanderthal unit X samples.

claims.claim: A flint flake partly covered in birch tar, about 50,000 years old, found off the present-day Dutch coast.
claims.found: A piece of birch tar enclosing a third of a flint flake: a hafted tool.
claims.dating: Radiocarbon dating and the geological source tie it to Middle Palaeolithic tools; about 50,000 years old.
claims.matters: Niekus et al. see complex technology. Schmidt et al. (2020) argue tar can be made simply, so the find does not show a complex method.

evidence.text: Schmidt et al. argue the Zandmotor data do not show a complex tar-making method, since simple burning of bark near stones also yields tar.

claims.claim: A Neanderthal cave site whose Micoquian layer 7a is dated to about 50,000 years ago.

source.citation: Dermeková et al. 2026, Journal of Paleolithic Archaeology

claims.found: Micoquian stone tools from several occupation areas; the cave has also yielded Neanderthal remains.
claims.dating: Layer 7a is dated to about 50,000 BP, as reported by Dermeková et al.; Rink et al. 1996 applied ESR dating to the Micoquian and Neanderthal remains.
claims.discovered: The studied artefacts were excavated between 1955 and 1977.
claims.matters: Kůlna is one of the main Neanderthal sites of Central Europe. Dermeková et al. used use-wear analysis to test older ideas of separate activity zones in the cave.

evidence.text: Rink et al. applied ESR dating to the Micoquian industry and the Neanderthal remains at Kůlna Cave.

source.citation: Rink et al. 1996, Journal of Archaeological Science

claims.question: neanderthal-extinction
claims.claim: Bones from Middle Palaeolithic layers once dated to 35,000–40,000 years ago, redated to more than 50,000 calendar years ago.

source.citation: Spindler et al. 2021, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: Bones from horizons of the Western Crimean Mousterian.
claims.dating: Single amino acid (hydroxyproline) radiocarbon dating gives ages over 50,000 cal BP, older than earlier bulk collagen dates.
claims.matters: Spindler et al. conclude there is little robust evidence of Neanderthals in Crimea after 40,000 years ago. Others give younger dates for sites such as Kiik-Koba and Zaskalnaya.

evidence.text: Majkić et al. give a date of about 35,000–37,000 cal BP for layer IV at Kiik-Koba, with a Neanderthal child burial.

claims.question: neanderthal-admixture
claims.claim: From the earliest modern human genomes, from Ranis and Zlatý kůň, about 45,000 to 49,000 years ago.
claims.wikipedia: Interbreeding between archaic and modern humans
claims.found: Genomes of six people from Ranis (Germany) and the woman from Zlatý kůň (Czechia), from one small, related group
claims.dating: Lengths of Neanderthal DNA segments, with radiocarbon dates of the Ranis bones, about 45,000 years
claims.discovered: Zlatý kůň skull found in 1950; Ranis bones dug in the 1930s and again 2016–2022
claims.matters: The oldest modern human genomes yet. Sümer et al. date mixing to about 45,000–49,000 years ago, shared by later non-Africans; Iasi et al. 2024 model a longer period.

evidence.text: Iasi et al. catalogued Neanderthal segments in more than 300 genomes and traced most gene flow to one extended period, 50,500 to 43,500 years ago.
Prüfer et al. found the Zlatý kůň woman’s Neanderthal segments longer than those of Ust’-Ishim, making her one of the earliest Eurasians after the expansion out of Africa.

source.citation: Prüfer et al. 2021, Nature Ecology & Evolution

evidence.text: Fu et al. found long Neanderthal segments in the 45,000-year-old Ust’-Ishim genome, placing the gene flow 7,000–13,000 years before he lived: somewhat earlier than this range.

claims.claim: A Dalmatian cave with Mousterian layers dated between about 49,000 and 39,000 calendar years ago, used by late Neanderthals.
claims.found: Mousterian stone tools in a sequence studied for its sediments, soils and magnetic properties.
claims.dating: Radiocarbon, soil and magnetic data place the sequence between about 49,000 and 39,000 cal BP; some radiocarbon dates were judged biased.
claims.matters: Boschian et al. found Neanderthals used the cave most during the earlier part, near Heinrich event 5, and only now and then later, when they shared it with carnivores.

evidence.text: Rink et al. dated the Mousterian levels at Mujina Pećina with ESR and AMS radiocarbon.

source.citation: Rink et al. 2002, Journal of Archaeological Science

claims.claim: Thirteen teeth from at least two adults, under 48,000 years old, with Neanderthal and modern-human traits.

source.citation: Compton et al. 2021, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: 13 teeth on a ledge behind a hearth in a Mousterian level (one now lost, one not human), and a later occipital fragment.
claims.dating: Dating of nearby sediments gives a probable age of less than 48,000 years.
claims.discovered: Excavated in 1910 and 1911.
claims.matters: Compton et al. find the teeth consistent with Neanderthals but with some modern-human traits, possibly shared ancestry.

claims.claim: A modern human woman’s skull over 45,000 years old, with about 3% Neanderthal ancestry.

source.citation: Prüfer et al. 2021, Nature Ecology & Evolution

claims.found: The skull of a woman whose genome was sequenced.
claims.dating: No reliable direct date; over 45,000 years from genetics, and kinship to Ranis implies about the age of Ranis13.
claims.matters: One of the earliest modern humans in Europe; her population left no detectable descendants (Prüfer et al.).

evidence.text: Sümer et al. found she was a distant relative of two Ranis individuals and belonged to the same small, isolated population.

claims.question: neanderthal-symbols
claims.claim: A fossil shell coated with hematite, brought from far away, in a Mousterian layer at least 47,600–45,000 years old.
claims.found: A fossil Aspa marginata shell with red hematite and striations, from more than 100 km away.
claims.dating: The Discoid Mousterian layer is dated to at least 47.6–45.0 cal ky BP.
claims.matters: Peresani et al. favour its use as a coloured pendant, part of Neanderthal symbolic culture before modern humans arrived.

evidence.text: Peresani et al. found cut and scrape marks only on the wings of vultures, eagles and other birds in the final Mousterian here, and read them as feather removal.
Finlayson et al. found a link between Neanderthals and raptors and corvids across many sites, and wing feather removal at Gibraltar.

claims.claim: A late Neanderthal from Les Cottés is one of five whose genomes were sequenced, all living 47,000 to 39,000 years ago.
claims.found: Neanderthal remains from a site with a complete Middle-to-Upper Palaeolithic transitional sequence (Talamo et al. 2012).
claims.dating: Hajdinjak et al. give 47,000–39,000 years for the five late Neanderthals; the site has its own radiocarbon sequence (Talamo et al. 2012).
claims.matters: Hajdinjak et al. found that genetic similarity among late Neanderthals follows geography. The site is one of the few with an unbroken Middle-to-Upper Palaeolithic sequence.

evidence.text: Devièse et al. place the disappearance of Neanderthals in Northwest Europe at 44,200–40,600 cal BP, within the range of the late Neanderthal genomes.
Fotiadou et al. note its mtDNA falls outside the lineage shared by nearly all other late Neanderthals.

claims.question: europe
claims.claim: The oldest securely dated Homo sapiens remains in Europe, about 44,000 to 46,000 years old.
claims.found: A tooth and bone fragments of Homo sapiens, identified by ancient proteins and DNA, with Initial Upper Palaeolithic tools and pendants
claims.dating: Radiocarbon of the human bones and of cut-marked animal bones, combined in a statistical model
claims.discovered: Dug in 1938 and 1971–1975; new excavations 2015–2017 by a Bulgarian–German team incl. Nikolay Sirakov, Tsenka Tsanova and Jean-Jacques Hublin
claims.matters: Directly dated human remains that put our species in Europe about 45,000 years ago, overlapping with Neanderthals there.

evidence.text: Fewlass et al. built a radiocarbon chronology from new animal and human bones and dated the Initial Upper Palaeolithic at the cave to 45,820–43,650 cal BP.

source.citation: Fewlass et al. 2020, Nature Ecology & Evolution

evidence.text: Hajdinjak et al. sequenced three Bacho Kiro individuals, 45,930–42,580 years old, and found Neanderthal ancestors a few generations back in each family.

claims.claim: The Deep Skull at Niah, among episodes of human activity from about 34,000 to 46,000 years ago.

source.citation: Barker et al. 2007, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: The ‘Deep Skull’ of a modern human, with evidence of hunting and processing of toxic plants in rainforest.
claims.dating: AMS radiocarbon on charcoal and uranium-series on fragments of the skull.
claims.discovered: Found in 1958 by Tom and Barbara Harrisson.
claims.matters: The oldest modern human in island Southeast Asia, showing people living in tropical rainforest early.

evidence.text: Curnoe et al. re-described the Deep Skull as most likely an older woman, not an adolescent male, and linked her to the earliest modern humans to settle Borneo.

source.citation: Curnoe et al. 2016, Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution

claims.claim: A bone fragment found by protein screening, radiocarbon dated to 45,000–46,000 years ago, whose mitochondrial genome is Neanderthal.
claims.found: One bone fragment about 5 cm long identified as human among 150 fragments by ZooMS; most bones were from hunted horses.
claims.dating: Radiocarbon dating of the fragment gave 46,000 to 45,000 years old, as reported by Pigott et al.
claims.matters: Pigott et al. report the first genetic data from a Crimean late Neanderthal and argue it shows long-distance connections across Eurasia.

evidence.text: Marks et al. reported earlier new excavations and results at Starosele, including on the Starosele child.

claims.claim: 99 Neanderthal bones dated to 45,500–40,500 years ago, with butchery marks; four were used to retouch stone tools.
claims.found: 99 newly identified Neanderthal remains with cut marks; four bones were used as retouchers.
claims.dating: Direct radiocarbon dates on the remains: 40,500–45,500 cal BP.
claims.matters: Rougier et al. call it the first clear evidence of Neanderthal cannibalism in northern Europe, and show varied treatment of the dead among late Neanderthals.

evidence.text: Defleur et al. inferred cannibalism at Moula-Guercy, France, from cut marks and bone treatment matching those on animals.
Hajdinjak et al. sequenced the Goyet Q56-1 genome, one of five late Neanderthals.
Fotiadou et al. added three more Goyet mtDNAs, all on the main late Neanderthal lineage.

claims.claim: The genome of a man who lived about 45,000 years ago, with Neanderthal ancestry from an admixture not long before.
claims.found: The left thigh bone of a man, from which a full, high-quality genome was read
claims.dating: Direct radiocarbon of the bone, about 45,000 years; the genome’s missing mutations give a similar age
claims.discovered: Found in 2008 by Nikolai Peristov, a carver, on the bank of the Irtysh River near Ust’-Ishim
claims.matters: The oldest modern human genome of its time. Its long Neanderthal segments put the mixing about 7,000–13,000 years before he lived, i.e. roughly 50,000–60,000 years ago.

evidence.text: Prüfer et al. compared the Zlatý kůň genome with the roughly 45,000-year-old Ust’-Ishim genome and found longer Neanderthal segments, suggesting she lived even earlier.

source.citation: Prüfer et al. 2021, Nature Ecology & Evolution

claims.question: europe
claims.claim: Bone fragments show Homo sapiens in Germany by 45,000 years ago, making the LRJ stone tools once credited to Neanderthals.
claims.found: Bone fragments identified as human by ancient proteins, with leaf-point tools.
claims.dating: Direct radiocarbon dating of the human bones; mitochondrial DNA and proteins confirm Homo sapiens.
claims.discovered: Excavated in 1932–1938 by Werner Hülle; re-excavated from 2016.
claims.matters: Small groups of our species reached cold northern Europe long before the last Neanderthals in the south-west.

evidence.text: Sümer et al. sequenced genomes from the roughly 45,000-year-old Ranis remains and found they belonged to a small, isolated population related to the Zlatý kůň woman.
Pederzani et al. studied isotopes in horse teeth and found the Homo sapiens at Ranis lived in cold steppe conditions, including a cold phase 45,000–43,000 years ago.

source.citation: Pederzani et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution

evidence.text: Smith et al. found that the Ranis Homo sapiens ate large land mammals in a cold steppe or tundra, on short visits by small, mobile groups.

source.citation: Smith et al. 2024, Nature Ecology & Evolution

claims.question: europe
claims.claim: Two milk teeth from Uluzzian layers, dated to about 45,000–43,000 years ago, attributed to modern humans; Zilhão et al. say Neanderthals.
claims.found: Two deciduous molars from layers with the Uluzzian, an early Upper Palaeolithic industry with shell beads.
claims.dating: A Bayesian model of dates on shell beads puts the teeth at about 45,000–43,000 calendar years ago.
claims.discovered: Excavated in 1963–66; the teeth were found in 1963 or 1964.
claims.matters: Benazzi et al. say modern humans made the Uluzzian. Zilhão et al. (2015) found disturbance and mixing, so the teeth cannot settle who made it.

evidence.text: Zilhão et al. found later lithics mixed into the Uluzzian layers and an unrecognised disturbance, so Neanderthal authorship remains the simplest reading.

claims.claim: Neanderthal 1, the type fossil, about 40,000 radiocarbon years old: roughly 42,500–44,300 calendar years.
claims.found: A skullcap and limb bones; new digs found fragments that fit onto it, and at least two more people.
claims.dating: Radiocarbon dating of the bones of Neanderthal 1 and a second individual, about 40,000 radiocarbon years; calibrated to calendar years with IntCal20 by this site.
claims.discovered: Found in 1856 by quarry workers; recognised by Johann Carl Fuhlrott.
claims.matters: The fossil that gave the Neanderthals their name and began the study of human fossils; its DNA was the first Neanderthal DNA read, in 1997.

evidence.text: Krings et al. extracted mitochondrial DNA from the type specimen found in 1856 and found it fell outside the variation of modern humans.
Richards and Schmitz measured stable isotopes in two hominins from the original Neanderthal site and found they ate mainly meat.

claims.question: neanderthal-extinction
claims.claim: Re-dated Neanderthals from Spy, Engis and Fonds-de-Forêt suggest Neanderthals vanished from Northwest Europe 44,200–40,600 years ago.
claims.found: Two adult Neanderthal skeletons and other remains, some found later on the slope below the cave.
claims.dating: Compound-specific radiocarbon dating with ancient DNA checks; earlier Spy dates were up to 10,000 years too young.
claims.discovered: The main fossils were found in 1885 and 1886.
claims.matters: Devièse et al. place the end earlier than before. Van Peer (2021) says the dated bones mostly come from old spoil, so the conclusion is premature.

evidence.text: Semal et al. had obtained four radiocarbon dates on the adult Spy Neanderthals suggesting survival to at least about 36,000 BP (uncalibrated).

source.citation: Semal et al. 2008, American Journal of Physical Anthropology

evidence.text: Van Peer argues that most dated bones come from waste of early digs on the slope, so the Spy stratigraphy makes the new end date premature.
Weyrich et al. found in Spy dental calculus a meat-heavy diet with woolly rhinoceros and wild sheep.
Hajdinjak et al. sequenced Spy 94a, a late Neanderthal genome.
Petr et al. sequenced the Spy 94a Y chromosome.

claims.claim: The Engis Neanderthal was re-dated in a study that places the end of Neanderthals in Northwest Europe at 44,200–40,600 years ago.
claims.found: Neanderthal remains from the Engis caves, directly dated in this study.
claims.dating: Direct radiocarbon dating with a compound-specific method; the 44.2–40.6 ka range is for the regional disappearance, not this bone alone.
claims.matters: Devièse et al. dated the Engis, Spy and Fonds-de-Forêt Neanderthals together to narrow the time of their disappearance.

evidence.text: Van Peer argues that the Spy stratigraphy makes the new regional end date premature, as most dated Spy bones come from old excavation waste.

claims.claim: A Neanderthal femur from Fonds-de-Forêt helps date the disappearance in Northwest Europe to 44,200–40,600 years ago.
claims.found: A Neanderthal femur.
claims.dating: Compound-specific radiocarbon dating.
claims.matters: Part of a refined chronology for the end of Neanderthals in Northwest Europe (Devièse et al.).

claims.claim: A Neanderthal lower third molar, the first Neanderthal remains reported from Greece, provisionally dated to about 38,000–44,000 years ago.

source.citation: Harvati et al. 2003, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: A lower third molar, LKH 1, with an anterior fovea and mid-trigonid crest.
claims.dating: Provisionally dated to about 38,000–44,000 years; the date is from a summary of Harvati et al., not checked against the abstract.
claims.matters: The tooth was reported with an Initial Upper Palaeolithic layer, which bears on whether late Neanderthals made early Upper Palaeolithic tools in Greece.

evidence.text: Smith et al. found the Lakonis molar formed faster and had thinner enamel than modern human molars, consistent with other Neanderthals.

source.citation: Smith et al. 2008, American Journal of Physical Anthropology

claims.claim: Stone tools hafted with bitumen in Mousterian levels about 42,000 years old, the first reported Middle Palaeolithic tools hafted with bitumen.
claims.found: A scraper and a Levallois flake with traces of black glue; no human remains.
claims.dating: Boëda et al. give the Mousterian levels as around 40,000 BC; the method is not stated in the abstract. Range approximate.
claims.discovered: Excavated in Syria’s El Kowm basin; the tools were analysed in 1996.
claims.matters: Chemistry shows the glue was heated bitumen used to fix handles. Boëda et al. speak of Middle Palaeolithic people; the link to Neanderthals rests on the Mousterian tools.

evidence.text: Griggo compared the animal bones of Dederiyeh, Umm el Tlel and Douara and read them as showing how well Neanderthals adapted to different environments.

claims.question: neanderthal-extinction
claims.claim: A Neanderthal milk canine with Zagros Mousterian tools, preliminarily dated to about 41,500–43,600 years ago.
claims.found: A deciduous (milk) canine of a Neanderthal child, found in place with Zagros Mousterian stone tools.
claims.dating: Preliminary dating of the layer to between about 43,600 and 41,500 years ago.
claims.discovered: Found in situ by a team led by Saman Heydari-Guran; reported in 2021.
claims.matters: Heydari-Guran et al. bring south-west Asia into the debate on Neanderthal extinction, until now based mostly on western Eurasia.

evidence.text: Zanolli et al. confirmed the Wezmeh 1 tooth, from the same region, as Neanderthal.

source.citation: Zanolli et al. 2019, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: At least twelve Neanderthals, about 43,000 years old, from a group that died about the same time; some bones carry human-made marks.
claims.found: Remains of 12 Neanderthals of all ages, some with cut marks, with Middle Palaeolithic stone tools.
claims.dating: Rosas et al. give about 43,000 years; a later ultrafiltered radiocarbon date gave 48,400 ± 3,200 radiocarbon years (uncalibrated).
claims.discovered: Systematically excavated since 2000.
claims.matters: A rare group sample. Lalueza-Fox et al. read its DNA as a sign that women moved between groups; Weyrich et al. found a plant-based diet in dental calculus.

evidence.text: Wood et al. obtained 48,400 ± 3,200 radiocarbon years BP (uncalibrated) on a bone, older than earlier inconsistent dates on the fossils.
Lalueza-Fox et al. found that the three adult males shared one mtDNA lineage while each adult female had a different one, suggesting patrilocality.
Weyrich et al. found no meat in El Sidrón dental calculus, but mushrooms, pine nuts and moss, and possible self-medication in one individual.
Mendez et al. analysed the El Sidrón 1253 Y chromosome and placed it outside modern human Y variation.

source.citation: Mendez et al. 2016, American Journal of Human Genetics

evidence.text: Slon et al. found Neanderthal mtDNA in El Sidrón sediment.

claims.question: neanderthal-extinction

place.name: Sima de las Palomas del Cabezo Gordo

claims.claim: Late Neanderthal remains, including several jaws, dated to 43,000–40,000 calendar years ago or less.
claims.found: Mandibles, teeth and hand bones from Middle Palaeolithic levels; eight partial mandibles in all.
claims.dating: Dated to ≤43,000–40,000 cal BP; Palomas 1 is older, about 50,000–60,000 cal BP (Walker et al. 2009).
claims.matters: Walker et al. see late Neanderthals in southern Iberia, perhaps with contact with modern humans to the north. Wood et al. (2013) question late southern Iberian dates.

evidence.text: Walker et al. described eight partial mandibles with Neanderthal traits, some among the latest Neanderthals at about 40,000 cal BP.

source.citation: Walker et al. 2009, American Journal of Physical Anthropology

evidence.text: Wood et al. found that late radiocarbon dates in southern Iberia should be treated as inaccurate unless rigorously pre-treated.

claims.question: neanderthal-symbols
claims.claim: A raven bone with seven deliberate notches from a Micoquian Neanderthal level dated to 38,000–43,000 calendar years ago.
claims.found: A raven radius with seven notches cut with a stone edge; two seem added to keep the spacing even.
claims.dating: The Micoquian level is dated to between 38,000 and 43,000 cal BP, as reported by Majkić et al.
claims.matters: Majkić et al. argue the notches were made to look regular, a sign of intent to make a pattern. d’Errico et al. report shaped ochre ‘crayons’ from Zaskalnaya V. Both read the finds as symbolic, which others may dispute.

evidence.text: d’Errico et al. studied ochre from Zaskalnaya V, VI and other sites and found pieces shaped like crayons and an engraved piece, which they read as symbolic use by Neanderthals.
Spindler et al. argue that, without reliable pretreatment, many Crimean radiocarbon dates should be taken as minimum ages.

source.citation: Spindler et al. 2021, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: Mungo Man and Mungo Lady, burials about 40,000 years old, the oldest human remains in Australia.
claims.found: Mungo I, a cremated woman, and Mungo III, a man buried with red ochre.
claims.dating: Optical (OSL) dating of 25 sediment samples: both burials at 40 ± 2 thousand years.
claims.discovered: Mungo I found in 1968 and Mungo III in 1974, both by Jim Bowler.
claims.matters: The world’s oldest known cremation and ochre burial; Mungo Man was returned to his Country in 2017.

evidence.text: Thorne et al. dated the Mungo 3 skeleton by ESR and uranium-series to 62,000 ± 6,000 years, much older than this claim.

source.citation: Thorne et al. 1999, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.question: neanderthal-admixture
claims.claim: Oase 1, a man 37,000 to 42,000 years old with a Neanderthal ancestor four to six generations back.
claims.found: The lower jaw of an early modern human; his genome is 6–9% Neanderthal.
claims.dating: Direct radiocarbon dating of the jaw; his ancestry from long Neanderthal segments in the genome.
claims.discovered: Found in 2002 by the cavers Ștefan Milota, Adrian Bîlgăr and Mihai Băilă.
claims.matters: Direct proof of mixing in Europe, not long before he lived; his group left no trace in later Europeans.

evidence.text: Trinkaus et al. described the Oase 1 jaw, directly dated to 34,000–36,000 radiocarbon years, as early modern human with a possibly Neanderthal feature.

claims.question: neanderthal-extinction
claims.claim: A rock shelter with the most detailed Middle to Upper Palaeolithic sequence in the Caucasus, where Adler et al. date the Neanderthal end to 42,000–39,000 calendar years ago.

source.citation: Adler et al. 2008, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: Late Middle Palaeolithic layers followed by early Upper Palaeolithic ones, with 76 dated samples.
claims.dating: After rejecting a quarter of the dates, modern humans appear about 38,000–34,000 radiocarbon years ago, 42,000–39,000 cal BP.
claims.matters: The site dates the turnover in the southern Caucasus, and the estimates differ: Adler et al. 42,000–39,000 cal BP, Pinhasi et al. 43,500–41,400, and Cullen et al. 47,500–44,200 for the end of the Middle Palaeolithic.

evidence.text: Pinhasi et al. modelled dates from western Georgia: the Middle Palaeolithic ended at Ortvala by 43,540–41,420 cal BP and at Sakajia 40,200–37,140 cal BP.

source.citation: Pinhasi et al. 2012, Journal of Human Evolution

evidence.text: Cullen et al. used a tephra from the Nemrut eruption and new dates to place the end of the Middle Palaeolithic at Ortvale Klde at about 47,500–44,200 cal BP.

source.citation: Cullen et al. 2021, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.question: neanderthal-burial
claims.claim: A Neanderthal child, La Ferrassie 8, laid in a pit; a bone from it is directly dated to 41,700–40,800 years ago.
claims.found: The skeleton of a two-year-old child in a pit dug into a sterile layer, in the great rock shelter that also held other Neanderthal skeletons.
claims.dating: Direct radiocarbon date (41.7–40.8 ka cal BP) on a bone identified by ZooMS and mtDNA, plus OSL dates on the sediment.
claims.discovered: First remains found in 1970 and most in 1973, in H. Delporte’s 1968–1973 excavations.
claims.matters: Balzeau et al. read the pit as a deliberate burial and the date as one of the latest for a Neanderthal. Critics such as Gargett argue articulated skeletons alone do not prove burial.

evidence.text: Gómez-Olivencia et al. found 47 new fragments of La Ferrassie 8 in museum collections and located the child in level M2 from the excavation notes.

source.citation: Gómez-Olivencia et al. 2015, Journal of Human Evolution

evidence.text: Gargett argued that articulated skeletons are not by themselves proof of deliberate Middle Palaeolithic burial, as natural cave processes can explain them.
Sandgathe et al. re-examined the Roc de Marsal child, another Dordogne case long accepted as a burial, and cast serious doubt on the pit being dug on purpose.

source.citation: Sandgathe et al. 2011, Journal of Human Evolution

evidence.text: Pelletier et al. found rabbits burrowed into the fill at nearby Regourdou, a possible oldest burial in western Europe, so bioturbation must be weighed at such sites.

source.citation: Pelletier et al. 2017, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.claim: Neanderthals disappear from Europe about 39,000 to 41,000 years ago.
claims.found: No single find: the last Mousterian and related tool layers at about 40 sites from Spain to Russia
claims.dating: New radiocarbon dates on bone and charcoal, with cleaner pre-treatment, combined in statistical models
claims.matters: Higham et al. find Neanderthals gone by about 39,000–41,000 years ago, after a few thousand years of overlap with modern humans.
claims.question: neanderthal-extinction

evidence.text: Zilhão et al. dated sites in Murcia and argued that the Neanderthal-associated Middle Palaeolithic lasted in southern Iberia until about 37,000 years ago.
Wood et al. re-dated southern Iberian sites with ultrafiltration and found the Zafarraya Neanderthals far older than thought, casting doubt on late survival there.
Spindler et al. redated Crimean bones to over 50,000 cal BP and conclude there is little robust evidence of Neanderthals in Crimea after 40,000 years ago.

source.citation: Spindler et al. 2021, Journal of Human Evolution

evidence.text: Pinhasi et al. revised Middle Palaeolithic dates in the Caucasus and argue Neanderthals did not survive there after 39,000 cal BP.

source.citation: Pinhasi et al. 2012, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.question: neanderthal-extinction
claims.claim: Neanderthal bones from Vindija redated to more than 40,000 years old, not 28,000–29,000.
claims.found: Fragmentary bones of several Neanderthals; one gave a high-quality genome in 2017.
claims.dating: Radiocarbon dating of hydroxyproline, an amino acid, extracted from the bones.
claims.discovered: Excavated in the 1970s and 1980s by Mirko Malez.
claims.matters: The earlier young dates made Vindija a late refuge; the new dates mean these Neanderthals probably did not overlap with modern humans.

evidence.text: Smith et al. directly dated two Vindija G1 Neanderthals to about 28,000 and 29,000 radiocarbon years, then the youngest dated Neanderthals.
Higham et al. re-dated the same fossils with ultrafiltration to about 32,000–33,000 radiocarbon years, and possibly earlier.
Prüfer et al. sequenced a 30-fold genome from a Neanderthal woman at Vindija, from samples 50,000–65,000 years old.

claims.question: neanderthal-extinction
claims.claim: An adult and a child, both Neanderthals, directly radiocarbon dated to about 39,700–39,100 and 36,100–35,400 calendar years ago.
claims.found: Remains of two Neanderthals, a young adult woman and a child of three to four, with a Late Mousterian industry.
claims.dating: Direct radiocarbon dates: 39,732–39,076 cal BP for the adult and 36,117–35,387 cal BP for the child, as quoted by Pálfi et al.
claims.discovered: Uncovered in 1932 near Cserépfalu, northern Hungary.
claims.matters: Mester et al. place these among the last Neanderthals of Central Europe. The child’s date is younger than the 39,000–41,000-year end that Higham et al. give for Neanderthals in Europe.

evidence.text: Pálfi et al. re-examined both skeletons and report signs of infection, including probable tuberculosis in the child, supported by lipid and DNA tests.

claims.question: chatelperronian
claims.claim: A late Neanderthal skeleton in a level with Châtelperronian tools, dated by thermoluminescence to about 36,300 ± 2,700 years ago; the link is disputed.
claims.found: A Neanderthal skeleton in level EJOP sup, which was attributed to the Châtelperronian, an early Upper Palaeolithic industry.
claims.dating: Thermoluminescence dates on 20 burnt flints; those near the skeleton gave 36,300 ± 2,700 years. Later directly radiocarbon dated (Hublin et al. 2012).
claims.matters: Mercier et al. and Hublin et al. see the Neanderthals as the makers of the Châtelperronian. Gravina et al. (2018) found no reliable association between the skeleton and those tools.

evidence.text: Hublin et al. directly dated the Saint-Césaire skeleton and say the result supports assigning the Châtelperronian to the latest western European Neanderthals.
Gravina et al. re-studied the lithics, refits and spatial data of the skeleton’s level and found no reliable evidence for a Neanderthal–Châtelperronian association.
Gargett questioned the reading of Saint-Césaire and other post-1960s finds as deliberate burials, arguing articulation alone is not proof.

claims.question: neanderthal-extinction
claims.claim: A directly dated late Neanderthal and 16 dates showing Neanderthals did not survive at Mezmaiskaya after about 39,000 calendar years ago.
claims.found: A late Neanderthal from a Late Middle Palaeolithic layer, in a cave with Middle and Upper Palaeolithic levels.
claims.dating: Direct date 39,700 ± 1,100 radiocarbon years (uncalibrated); Bayesian modelling puts the end of the Middle Palaeolithic before 39,000 cal BP.
claims.matters: Pinhasi et al. reject a late survival here. Ovchinnikov et al. once dated a Mezmaiskaya Neanderthal to about 29,000 radiocarbon years. Its DNA helped show a turnover among late Neanderthals.

evidence.text: Ovchinnikov et al. analysed mtDNA from a Mezmaiskaya Neanderthal, which radiocarbon dating then put at about 29,000 years old, making it seem one of the last.
Hajdinjak et al. sequenced late Neanderthals 39,000–47,000 years old and, comparing them with an older Caucasus Neanderthal, found signs of a population turnover.
Doronicheva et al. compared tools from Mezmaiskaya and Saradj-Chuko, from MIS 5 to MIS 3, and identify two culturally different Neanderthal populations in contact.
Andreeva et al. found Mezmaiskaya 3’s mtDNA closest to Mezmaiskaya 1 and Stajnia S5000.

claims.question: tabun-age
claims.claim: The Tabun C1 woman dated directly by uranium-series to about 34,000 years, which would make her one of the last Neanderthals of the Levant.

source.citation: Simpson et al. 1998, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.found: The mandible and a femur of the Tabun C1 skeleton, sampled for dating.
claims.dating: Gamma-ray uranium-series: jaw 34 ± 5 ka with early uptake; femur 19 ± 2 ka, or 33 ± 4 ka with linear uptake.
claims.discovered: Garrod and Bate placed the skeleton in layer B or C of their sequence.
claims.matters: Simpson et al. say this would mean Neanderthals survived as late in the Levant as in Europe. The ages depend on how the bones took up uranium, and Grün & Stringer 2000 date her to about 122,000.

evidence.text: Grün and Stringer revised the ESR chronology and analysed teeth of Tabun C1, giving an older age of about 122,000 years (from a summary; abstract not seen).

source.citation: Grün & Stringer 2000, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.question: neanderthal-extinction
claims.claim: A Mousterian layer no more than 37,100 years old, which Zilhão et al. read as late Neanderthal survival in southern Iberia; disputed.
claims.found: Mousterian layers, and earlier a perforated scallop shell painted with an orange mix of goethite and hematite.
claims.dating: Radiocarbon and luminescence dating: Mousterian layer I-k can be no more than 37,100 years old.
claims.matters: Zilhão et al. see an ‘Ebro frontier’ that kept Neanderthals in the south 3,000 years longer. Wood et al. (2013) found most late southern Iberian dates unreliable.

evidence.text: Zilhão et al. reported a perforated Pecten shell painted on its outer side with goethite and hematite, abandoned after breaking.
Wood et al. found most southern Iberian dates unreliable, leaving Cueva Antón as the only possible site for late Neanderthal survival there.

claims.question: neanderthal-extinction
claims.claim: A Neanderthal child burial and an engraved flint, in a layer dated to about 35,000–37,000 calendar years ago, a date others treat as a minimum.
claims.found: A Neanderthal child burial, the Kiik-Koba 1 adult and a flint flake with deliberate engraving on its cortex, in layer IV.
claims.dating: Layer IV, with a para-Micoquian industry, dated to about 35,000–37,000 cal BP, as reported by Majkić et al.
claims.matters: If right, the date makes Kiik-Koba one of the latest Neanderthal sites. Spindler et al. argue many Crimean dates should be read as minimum ages, with little robust evidence of Neanderthals there after 40,000 years ago.

evidence.text: Trinkaus et al. describe the Kiik-Koba 1 Neanderthal, a man of about 40, with healed injuries and other lesions common among Neanderthals.

source.citation: Trinkaus et al. 2008, American Journal of Physical Anthropology

evidence.text: Spindler et al. redated Kabazi II bones from 35,000–40,000 to over 50,000 cal BP, and advise treating other Crimean dates as minimum ages.

source.citation: Spindler et al. 2021, Journal of Human Evolution

claims.question: neanderthal-extinction
claims.claim: Neanderthals at Gorham’s Cave until about 28,000, possibly 24,000, radiocarbon years ago (roughly 33,000–27,700 calendar years); disputed.
claims.found: Mousterian stone tools and hearths in a sea cave, with no Neanderthal bones in the late layers.
claims.dating: Radiocarbon dating of charcoal, given in radiocarbon years; calibrated to calendar years with IntCal20 by this site.
claims.discovered: Dug from the 1990s by Clive Finlayson’s team, Gibraltar Museum; first excavated in the 1950s.
claims.matters: Finlayson et al. see a last refuge in the far south; Wood et al. (2013) found the late southern Iberian dates unreliable when retested.

evidence.text: Higham et al. modelled radiocarbon dates from 40 sites from Russia to Spain and found the Mousterian ended across Europe by 41,030–39,260 cal BP.
Wood et al. found that most southern Iberian sites could not be reliably dated and that late radiocarbon dates there should be treated as inaccurate unless rigorously pre-treated.
Zilhão et al. found Neanderthal-associated layers in Murcia younger than 37,100 years, in agreement, they say, with evidence from Gibraltar.
Rodríguez-Vidal et al. report a deeply cut cross-hatched engraving in the bedrock, older than 39 cal kyr and sealed by Mousterian layer IV.
Stringer et al. report seal, dolphin, fish and molluscs at nearby Vanguard Cave and marine mammals in Mousterian levels at Gorham’s Cave.
Finlayson et al. found a taphonomic link between Neanderthals and raptors and corvids at Gorham’s, Vanguard and Ibex Caves, with wing feathers removed.

claims.question: americas
claims.claim: Human footprints dated to 21,000 to 23,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Maximum; later dated again by other methods, with the same result.

source.citation: Bennett et al. 2021, Science; Pigati et al. 2023, Science

claims.found: Human footprints, many of teenagers and children, in layers of an old lakeshore with mammoth and ground sloth tracks
claims.dating: Radiocarbon of seeds of the water plant Ruppia above and below the prints; later radiocarbon of conifer pollen and luminescence of quartz
claims.discovered: Found by park staff, including David Bustos; excavated by teams led by Matthew Bennett and Bustos
claims.matters: If right, people were in North America during the Last Glacial Maximum. Madsen et al. 2022 argued the seed ages could be too old; Pigati et al. 2023 found other methods agree.

evidence.text: Madsen et al. argued that reservoir effects may have made the Ruppia seed ages thousands of years too old, and called for independent dating.
Pigati et al. dated land-plant pollen and quartz grains from the same layers and found the original age framework robust.
Rhode et al. argued that the newer pollen and luminescence ages may also be maximum ages, implying a significantly younger age for the footprints.
Holliday et al. traced the track-bearing layers into an old lake record and, with 26 radiocarbon dates from two independent labs, supported a Last Glacial Maximum age.

claims.question: americas
claims.claim: A camp about 14,500 years old, far south, before Clovis.
claims.found: Monte Verde II: remains of a camp with hearths, wooden posts, stone tools, plants and gomphothere bones, kept by peat
claims.dating: Radiocarbon of wood, charcoal, bone and plant remains
claims.discovered: Found in 1975 after logging cut a creek bank; excavated from 1977 by a team led by Tom Dillehay
claims.matters: Accepted by many after 1997 as evidence of people in South America before Clovis. Dillehay et al. 2015 also report older traces, about 18,500 years, which are debated.

evidence.text: Surovell et al. found an 11,000-year-old volcanic ash below the archaeological layer and argued Monte Verde cannot be older than the Middle Holocene, 8,200–4,200 years ago.
Dillehay et al. replied that these claims contain errors and flaws, and upheld the reading of Monte Verde II as a late Pleistocene camp of about 14,500 years ago.
Pino and Dillehay dated 43 samples from sediments over the site and placed the earliest layers sealing the camp at about 14,550 cal BP.
Meltzer et al. reported that Paleoindian specialists who examined the collections and visited the site agreed Monte Verde II is archaeological and 12,500 years old.

claims.question: americas
claims.claim: The Clovis culture, about 12,750 to 13,050 years ago; long held to be the first people in the Americas.
claims.found: Fluted spear points (Clovis points) and other tools, at Blackwater Draw with mammoth bones; similar sites across North America
claims.dating: Re-dated radiocarbon of bone, charcoal and seeds from Clovis sites, calibrated to calendar years
claims.discovered: Blackwater Draw finds reported by Ridgely Whiteman in 1929; excavated from 1932 by Edgar B. Howard and others
claims.matters: Waters and Stafford found Clovis lasted only a few centuries, too short to have spread from one first group; with sites like Monte Verde, this weighs against ‘Clovis first’.

evidence.text: Waters et al. re-examined the Clovis radiocarbon record and again placed the complex at 13,050 to 12,750 cal yr BP.
Haynes et al. argued the re-dating gave useful ages for some Clovis sites but did not definitively establish how long Clovis lasted.
Sánchez et al. dated a Clovis site with gomphothere remains in Sonora, Mexico, to about 13,390 cal BP, earlier than this range.

claims.question: east-asia
claims.claim: Ancient DNA and direct radiocarbon dates on Fuyan teeth show them to be from the last 11,700 years.
claims.found: Human teeth from Fuyan and four other caves in southern China claimed as early modern humans.
claims.dating: Direct radiocarbon on human teeth, ancient DNA, OSL of sediments and radiocarbon of charcoal and animal teeth.
claims.matters: Sun et al. place our species in southern China within 45,000–50,000 years ago; Martinón-Torres et al. (2021) reply that the teeth dated were misidentified and of unreliable context.

evidence.text: Liu et al. first dated the 47 Fuyan teeth to more than 80,000 years, with an inferred maximum of 120,000, from flowstone and fauna in the cave.

claims.claim: The Forbes’ Quarry skull from Gibraltar kept small amounts of Neanderthal DNA.
claims.found: A partial cranium (Gibraltar 1), one of the first Neanderthal remains found.
claims.dating: No absolute date; Bokelmann et al. infer from genetics that it predates late Neanderthals.
claims.matters: DNA survived in a warm coastal climate close to Africa (Bokelmann et al.).

evidence.text: Slimak et al. found Thorin’s mtDNA most closely related to Forbes’ Quarry.

claims.claim: The Devil’s Tower skull from Gibraltar yielded a little Neanderthal nuclear DNA from a male.
claims.found: A partial cranium (Gibraltar 2).
claims.dating: No date in the source.
claims.matters: One of the first Neanderthal remains found, now with DNA (Bokelmann et al.).

claims.claim: Sediments at Galería de las Estatuas hold Neanderthal nuclear and mtDNA pointing to a turnover about 100,000 years ago.
claims.found: Neanderthal DNA in cave sediments, without skeletons.
claims.dating: Not given in the abstract.
claims.matters: Shows population genetics from dirt alone (Vernot et al.).

evidence.text: Slimak et al. place two Estatuas mtDNAs in a clade with Thorin and Forbes’ Quarry.

claims.claim: Sediments at Trou Al’Wesse contain Neanderthal mtDNA though no Neanderthal bones were found in its Pleistocene layers.
claims.found: Neanderthal mtDNA in sediment; Late Mousterian artefacts and cut-marked animal bones.
claims.dating: Not given in the source text read.
claims.matters: Sediment DNA can show who used a site without skeletons (Slon et al.).

claims.claim: A Neanderthal femur from Les Rochers-de-Villeneuve dates to about 40,700 radiocarbon years (uncalibrated).
claims.found: A partial femur, found in 2002.
claims.dating: Radiocarbon about 40,700 BP; only uncalibrated years given.
claims.discovered: Discovered in 2002.
claims.matters: One of the most recent Middle Palaeolithic Neanderthals; level shows alternating human and hyena use (Beauval et al.).

claims.claim: A Neanderthal neonate from Trou Magrite gave mtDNA of the late Neanderthal lineage.
claims.found: A neonate, one of two Neanderthal remains from the site.
claims.dating: Not directly dated; context uncertain.
claims.matters: Its mtDNA suggests it belongs with late Neanderthals (Fotiadou et al.).

claims.claim: Three pre-MIS 3 Neanderthals from a Quina Mousterian context at Tourtoirac gave mtDNA.
claims.found: Remains of three Neanderthals.
claims.dating: Pre-MIS 3; no calendar range in the text read.
claims.matters: More mtDNA diversity than at single late sites (Fotiadou et al.).
